pool.q: A 4-year-old is referred for unilateral hypopyon. Perinatal history is unremarkable, and there is no significant family history. Systemic workup for infectious and inflammatory disorders is noncontributory. What should be the next step?

options.c: pars plana needle biopsy for flow cytometry
options.d: examination under anesthesia with ultrasonography imaging

pool.rationale:
Hypopyon and uveitis in the pediatric population is retinoblastoma until proven otherwise.
The diagnosis of retinoblastoma can usually be made during a dilated indirect ophthalmoscopic examination performed under anesthesia; the characteristic finding is a chalky, off-white retinal mass with a soft, friable consistency.
Ocular ultrasonography shows a solid intraocular tumor with characteristic intratumoral calcifications.
CT scan is not recommended in patients with suspected retinoblastoma, because there is a risk of radiation-induced secondary cancers in patients with germinal disease. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can be helpful to confirm the presence of an intraocular mass.
Sixty (60) percent of children with retinoblastoma have the unilateral, non-germline, and non-heritable form of the disease. In cases of unilateral disease, molecular/genetic testing should be done initially on tumor cells (if available from enucleation) to identify the specific RB1 mutation. It is not indicated in the initial work up for diagnosis.
Needle biopsy is contraindicated in retinoblastoma, as seeding of the tumor can occur.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What phase of the immune response arc is constituted by the initial recognition, transport, and presentation of antigenic substances to the adaptive immune system?
pool.rationale: Following ingestion of antigen, antigen-presenting cells (APCs) migrate via afferent lymphatics to lymph nodes. In the APCs, enzymatic digestion of proteins within endocytic vesicles produces short amino acid chains of 7–11 amino acids: the antigenic epi­topic fragments. Each antigenic fragment is combined with a groove-shaped HLA peptide residing on the APC surface, and this surface complex forms a unique epitope. The combination of peptide and HLA protein is recognized by the T-lymphocyte receptors CD4 and CD8.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Mycophenolate mofetil is in the same class of immunosuppressive drugs as what agent?
pool.rationale:
Mycophenolate mofetil is an antimetabolite, as are methotrexate and azathioprine; it inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase and DNA replication. Methotrexate is a folic acid analogue and also an inhibitor of dihydrofolate reductase. Azathioprine is a purine nucleoside analogue that has its effects on DNA replication and RNA transcription.
Cyclosporine is a calcineurin inhibitor (inhibits T-cell signaling); cyclophosphamide is an alkylating agent; and infliximab is tumor necrosis factor-alpha inhibitor and is in the group of biologic response modifiers.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What systemic disease should be considered in a previously healthy adult patient from Mexico with uveitis, seizures, and calcifications in the central nervous system (CNS) on computed tomography (CT) scan?
pool.rationale:
Taenia solium infection)

Cysticercosis is the most common ocular tapeworm infection caused by Taenia solium, which is endemic to Mexico, Central and South America, Eastern Europe, Africa, and India. The eye and CNS are commonly affected.
It may involve the eye and the adnexae. Subretinal space may harbor the parasite. These larvae may cause exudative retinal detachment, perforate the retina, and invade the vitreous cavity. Larvae can be seen undulating in the vitreous or subretinal space.
Neurocysticercosis presents with seizures and, less commonly, headaches. In developing countries, this is one of the most common causes of seizures. Cysts located within the ventricles of the brain can block the outflow of cerebrospinal fluid and present with symptoms of increased intracranial pressure.
SSPE is a fatal, progressive degenerative disease of the central nervous system that usually occurs 7 to 10 years after natural measles virus infection. Computed tomography of the head may demonstrate atrophy and scarring. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain may be normal. The most characteristic fundus finding in these patients is chorioretinitis.
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a severe demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that is caused by reactivation of the polyomavirus JC (JC virus).
The typical appearance of PML on neuroimaging studies consists of symmetric or asymmetric multifocal areas of white matter demyelination that do not conform to cerebrovascular territories.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What oral therapy is preferred for treatment of cytomegalovirus (CMV)-associated retinitis?
pool.rationale: Oral valganciclovir (900 mg twice daily for 3 weeks for induction, followed by once daily for 3-6 months) or intravenous ganciclovir (5 mg/kg twice daily for 2 weeks, followed by maintenance oral therapy), along with initiation of potent combination antiretroviral therapy, are the mainstays of treatment for CMV retinitis. Foscarnet (intravenous or intravitreal) can also be used. Acyclovir (or valacyclovir) is not used in the treatment of CMV retinitis. Cidofovir does have anti-CMV activity, but this agent is not used orally.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Aside from effector blockade and anterior chamber–associated immune deviation, what is the major mechanism that affords immune privilege to the cornea?
pool.rationale: Cytokines and complement help recruit immune mediators to the central cornea, which is otherwise relatively devoid of immune effectors. Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue is responsible for conjunctival antigenic processing, but the effector limb of this system can spill over onto the corneal surface and recruit immune effectors to the cornea. Limbal physiology is the mechanism that keeps immune effectors from reaching the central cornea (ie, makes the cornea immune privileged), mainly by serving as a barrier to vascularization of the cornea, which would provide great immune access to the central cornea, but at the cost of severe reduction in vision.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 25-year-old woman was recently diagnosed with pars planitis. Her visual acuity is 20/20 OD, 20/50 OS. The examination reveals vitreous cells and cystoid macular edema (CME) in the left eye. What is the most appropriate patient management plan?

options.c: argon laser treatment of the peripheral retina

pool.rationale: Sub-Tenon corticosteroid injection is the most appropriate patient management plan for the intraocular inflammation and CME present in the left eye. Cytotoxic agents, such as methotrexate, and invasive procedures, such as vitrectomy, are generally not indicated as first-line treatment in this setting. Argon laser treatment of the peripheral retina may be indicated for peripheral retinal neovascularization, which occurs in a minority of cases.

pool.q: What factor is associated with vision loss in patients with ocular sarcoidosis?

options.a: delay of more than 1 year in presentation to a uveitis specialist
options.c: anterior uveitis associated with nummular corneal infiltrates
options.d: positive ACE and serum lysozyme levels

pool.rationale: Referral to a uveitis specialist should be strongly considered for patients who have ocular sarcoidosis that is difficult to control. The need for immunomodulatory therapy (IMT) is not necessarily associated with vision loss; patients receiving such treatment might eventually fare better than patients who receive intermittent treatment for flare-ups. Findings such as elevated ACE and serum lysozyme levels, anterior uveitis, and nummular corneal infiltrates occur in ocular sarcoidosis, but they are not specifically associated with an increased risk of vision loss.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient being treated for HLA-B27-associated uveitis is responding to topical steroids but develops elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) on the sixth day of therapy. What is the best next step in management?
pool.rationale:
Early in the course of all cases of uveitis, the first priority is the control of intraocular inflammation, even if the IOP is high. The dosage and frequency of corticosteroid use should not be decreased prematurely.
If there is elevated intraocular pressure at any time during the treatment of uveitis, ocular anti-hypertensive agents (such as brimonidine) should be employed as soon as possible. However, pilocarpine should be avoided in all uveitic cases because it is pro-inflammatory and may aggravate synechiae formation. Similarly, prostaglandin-analogues are also avoided initially as a first-line treatment in uveitis-induced IOP elevation.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common fundus autofluorescence (FAF) imaging pattern in a patient with multifocal choroiditis?

options.b: multiple punctate hypoautofluorescent spots that may be more numerous than clinical appearance
options.d: hyperautofluorescent areas that correspond to areas of blockage on fluorescein angiogram (FA)

pool.rationale: The most common fundus autofluorescence finding in multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis is multiple punctate hypoautofluorescent spots. Some spots correspond to areas of chorioretinal atrophy, but many more spots may be discerned than are visible on fundus examination. Central hypoautofluoresence with peripheral hyperautofluorescence is a common FAF pattern in AZOOR (acute zonal occult outer retinopathy). Hyperautofluorescent areas that correspond to areas of blockage on fluorescein angiogram (FA) may be seen in acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient has decreased vision from a vitreous hemorrhage, and no retinal breaks can be found. After the hemorrhage clears, the retinal appearance is abnormal, as shown in the image. What is the most likely systemic diagnosis?
pool.rationale: The image depicts an area of midperipheral venous sheathing and sclerosis, suggestive of a systemic vasculitis. Among the answer choices given (including toxoplasmosis, ankylosing spondylitis, and Bartonella henselae infection), ANCA-associated vasculitis is the only one that suggests the presence of a systemic vasculitis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient from sub-Saharan Africa presents with mild anterior uveitis; papular skin lesions on the buttocks, waist, and shoulders; and conjunctival nodules. There is mild retinal pigment epithelial atrophy and a suggestion of optic atrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Onchocerciasis is one of the leading causes of blindness ("river blindness") in Central America, South America, and sub-Saharan Africa. It is caused by the parasite Onchocerca volvulus and is transmitted by the black flies of Simulium genus.
The larvae develop into mature worms that migrate to the skin and form subcutaneous nodules.
Any part of the eye, from the conjunctiva and cornea to the uvea and posterior segment, including the retina and optic nerve, may be involved. Microfilariae can even be observed swimming in the anterior chamber. The microfilariae migrate to the surface of the cornea, causing punctate keratitis, or sclerosing keratitis if the infection is chronic. Over time, the entire cornea may become opaque, thus leading to blindness. Mild to severe anterior uveitis, secondary glaucoma, and cataract may develop. Posterior segment findings may include early disruption of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), as well as pigment dispersion and atrophy. These may ensue in severe chorioretinal atrophy and optic atrophy.
Behçet disease classically affects young males who have a history of oral ulcers and have explosive inflammatory ocular response.
HIV/AIDS retinopathy usually is characterized by microvascular changes, such as cotton-wool spots, microaneurysms, and telangiectasias, and later subsequently described with secondary opportunistic infections.
Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease presents as a panuveitis with a prodromal, uveitis, convalescent, and recurrent stage.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with decreased vision in the right eye. The result of the fundus examination is seen in Figure 1. What is the most likely cause of decreased vision?
pool.rationale: CNV within the macula is the main cause of decreased vision in OHS. CNV within choroidal scars develops in approximately 0.8% of patients with OHS. If these scars develop within the macula, there is a 25% chance of developing maculopathy with subsequent vision loss within 3 years. Optic atrophy, cataract, and peripheral retinal degeneration are not features of OHS.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In a patient with ocular toxoplasmosis, what physical examination finding should prompt HIV testing?
pool.rationale:
Toxoplasmosis typically presents as a focal white retinitis, often adjacent to a pigmented chorioretinal scar with overlying vitritis. Multiple active lesions in one or both eyes are rare and should prompt HIV testing. HIV-positive patients have a high rate of central nervous system (CNS) involvement and should undergo magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with contrast.
Granulomatous anterior uveitis, macular involvement, and segmental perivascular plaques can all be seen in toxoplasmosis and are not specific to the presentation of toxoplasmosis in immunocompromised individuals.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What laboratory parameter requires regular monitoring with use of systemic cyclosporine?
pool.rationale: Nephrotoxicity and hypertension are the major systemic side effects of cyclosporine. Serum creatinine should be monitored regularly with patients taking cyclosporine, and dosage adjustments are needed if it rises 30% or more above baseline. Sustained elevation may require discontinuation of this medication. Systemic hypertension is another major side effect of cyclosporine, and the blood pressure of patients taking cyclosporine should be checked at each clinic visit. Other side effects include gum hyperplasia, and hirsutism.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Within what ethnic group or geographic region is birdshot chorioretinopathy most prevalent?
pool.rationale: Birdshot chorioretinopathy is most prevalent in individuals of northern European descent. Typically diagnosed in the fourth to sixth decade of life, this entity affects women more frequently than men.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In what stage of the disease does Lyme disease (LD)–associated intermediate uveitis occur most commonly?
pool.rationale: The most common ocular manifestation of early stage 1 LD is follicular conjunctivitis. LD-associated uveitis occurs most commonly in stage 2 disease and less commonly in stage 3. It can manifest as anterior, intermediate, and posterior uveitis and as panuveitis; intermediate is the most common. Granulomatous anterior chamber reaction, severe vitritis, papillitis, retinal vasculitis, neuroretinitis, and choroiditis with exudative retinal detachment can also occur.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A previously healthy 47-year-old patient presents with unilateral decreased vision of 20/80 and grade 3+ cell and flare. What additional evaluation must be performed before a diagnosis of anterior uveitis is established?
pool.rationale: Anterior uveitis is an anatomic classification of uveitis that requires the exclusion of posterior segment inflammation; several vision-threatening causes of uveitis can be misdiagnosed if a dilated fundus examination is not performed. These include acute retinal necrosis, Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis, and endogenous endophthalmitis. The appearance of the anterior segment does not predict the presence or absence of posterior segment pathology, making dilated fundus exam necessary for any patient with intraocular inflammation of unknown cause. While review of systems and investigations such as radiographs of the sacroiliac (SI) joint and HLA B27 testing may be needed to establish the cause or systemic association of the uveitis, it is not useful in establishing the anatomical diagnosis of the uveitis or in differentiating between anterior, intermediate, posterior, and panuveitis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What ocular inflammatory disorder is primarily associated with the activation of mast cells via immunoglobulin E (IgE) antibodies?
pool.rationale: Mast cells act as major effector cells in IgE-mediated, immune-triggered inflammatory reactions, especially allergy or immediate hypersensitivity. Vernal conjunctivitis usually involves many conjunctival mast cells; these mast cells have IgE antibodies bound to cell-surface Fc receptors, and antigen binding results in degranulation of these cells. Preformed substances released upon degranulation include histamine, serotonin, and proteases. Eicosanoids such as leukotrienes are also produced, adding to the inflammatory effects of mast cell activation. Juvenile xanthogranuloma is a histiocytic process affecting mainly the skin and eyes, and, in rare instances, viscera. Patients usually present before age 1 with characteristic skin lesions that are reddish yellow. Histologic investigation shows large histiocytes with foamy cytoplasm and Touton giant cells. The pathogenesis of scleritis may involve cell-mediated immunity and immune complex deposition. Contact hypersensitivity dermatitis is a manifestation of cell-mediated immunity and does not rely upon immunoglobulins.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with large keratic precipitates, posterior synechiae, and vitritis. A purified protein derivative (PPD) test is placed as part of the workup and is read 48 hours later at 6 mm induration. Under what condition would this PPD be considered positive?

options.a: The patient had contact with an individual with active tuberculosis.
options.b: The patient is a healthcare worker.
options.d: The patient has a history of intravenous drug abuse.

pool.rationale: An induration of at least 5 mm is considered positive in those exposed to active tuberculosis, those with HIV infection, or in patients with radiographic evidence of healed tuberculous lesions. An induration of 10 mm or more is considered positive in high-risk groups, which include patients with diabetes, those with renal failure, those on systemic immunomodulatory therapy, immigrants from TB-endemic areas, and health care workers. In this scenario, the PPD from the patient with an induration of 6 mm and recent contact with a person with active TB would be considered positive.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What histopathologic feature is most characteristic of sarcoid uveitis?
pool.rationale:
Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disorder. It frequently involves lymph nodes, skin, eyes, central nervous system (CNS), bones and joints, liver, and heart. Ocular involvement may occur in about 50% of patients. The basic pathologic lesion is noncaseating granuloma; also found are multinucleated giant cells, Schaumann bodies, and asteroid bodies.
Ocular presentations of sarcoidosis are chronic granulomatous iridocyclitis, nummular corneal infiltrates, band keratopathy, iris granulomas, vitritis, optic nerve granuloma, and periphlebitis.
Necrotizing vasculitis is more consistent with granulomatosis, polyangiitis, and Behçet disease.
Touton giant cells are seen in juvenile xanthogranuloma. This is a histiocytic process and involves skin, eyes, and viscera. Patients may present with spontaneous hyphema.
The granulomas of tuberculosis (TB) contain necrosis, called caseating tubercules/granulomas.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most likely finding in a person who is HLA-A29 positive?

options.b: ovoid, yellowish chorioretinal lesions distributed mostly around the optic nerve

pool.rationale: While over 90% of patients with birdshot chorioretinopathy are positive for HLA-A29, most people who are HLA-A29 positive will never manifest birdshot chorioretinopathy and will have a normal eye examination. Approximately 8% of the general population in the US is positive for HLA-A29, and fewer than 1 in 10,000 individuals in the US will manifest birdshot chorioretinopathy. Patients with birdshot chorioretinopathy may have creamy, ovoid chorioretinal lesions, retinal vasculitis, or macular edema.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 42-year-old Iranian man reports decreased vision in his right eye over the past 3 days. He does not endorse significant pain or discomfort, but on review of systems, the ophthalmologist discovers that he also has ulcers on the inside of his mouth. For which HLA haplotype would the patient most likely be positive?
pool.rationale:
The clinical presentation is one of Behçet disease. Panuveitis with occlusive retinal vasculitis is the most common presentation. HLA-B51 is commonly associated with Behçet disease with ocular manifestations. However, the diagnosis of Behçet is clinical, and laboratory tests are of little value in confirming the diagnosis.
HLA-A29 is more common in patients with birdshot chorioretinopathy, HLA-B27 is associated with acute anterior uveitis, and HLA-DR4 is weakly associated with Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient with necrotizing scleritis is found to have antibodies directed against proteinase 3. What disease is most likely to be associated with this finding?
pool.rationale: Testing for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) involves 2 techniques: (1) immunofluorescent testing, which evaluates for the presence of cytoplasmic or perinuclear immunofluorescence patterns (c-ANCA and p-ANCA, respectively), and (2) testing for the specific antibodies that cause each immunofluorescent pattern. Antibodies to proteinase 3 (PR3-ANCA) are associated with c-ANCA, and antibodies to myeloperoxidase (MPO-ANCA) are associated with p-ANCA. Tests for PR3-ANCA and c-ANCA are sensitive and specific for granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Positivity for MPO-ANCA and p-ANCA is more commonly associated with microscopic polyangiitis. Approximately 50% of patients with Churg-Strauss syndrome test positive for ANCA; they are typically, but not uniformly, MPO-ANCA positive. In a patient with antibodies to proteinase 3, the most likely associated disease will be granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What stage of Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome is most likely to be associated with exudative retinal detachments?
pool.rationale: The acute uveitic stage is typically associated with exudative retinal detachments. By definition, the prodromal stage is characterized by systemic symptoms such as a flulike syndrome and headaches prior to the development of clinically apparent ophthalmic disease. The convalescent stage occurs weeks to months after the exudative retinal detachments have resolved; patients can develop gradual depigmentation in the fundus and findings such as vitiligo, alopecia, and poliosis. The chronic recurrent stage is associated with repeated bouts of anterior uveitis that can lead to significant structural damage, but it is not commonly associated with recurrence of the exudative retinal detachments.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the first-line oral antibiotic in the treatment of ocular Lyme disease (LD)?
pool.rationale:
Ocular LD is typically treated in the same manner as central nervous system (CNS) LD. The antibiotics doxycycline, amoxicillin, and ceftriaxone (and other penicillin family members) are most effective in treating ocular LD.
Chloramphenicol, a broad-spectrum antibiotic, is typically administered intravenously and orally but is also available as an ophthalmic suspension outside the US. Chloramphenicol has been used to treat intraocular rickettsial infections (gram-negative arthropod-borne bacteria), but not the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, the etiologic agent causing LD.
Ciprofloxacin, a fluoroquinolone, has good coverage against gram-negative bacteria, but it is not as effective in treating spirochetal infections as doxycycline and the penicillin-family antibiotics.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with scleritis. What clinical feature is more suggestive of an infectious rather than a noninfectious etiology?

options.c: Site of inflammation is status post pterygium excision.

pool.rationale: Surgery and trauma are risk factors for infectious scleritis, which occurs at the site of the previous surgery. Scleritis with thin, necrotic, or avascular sclera may be caused by a noninfectious process.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What topical corticosteroid medication is most likely to cause a corticosteroid-response elevation in IOP?
pool.rationale: Of the choices listed, prednisolone acetate 1% demonstrates the greatest effect of decreasing intraocular inflammation, and the greatest effect of increasing IOP. Rimexolone has a slightly less potent effect. Fluorometholone is a very potent corticosteroid, but penetrates poorly into the eye and therefore is less likely to result in an increase in IOP. Loteprednol is also less likely to raise IOP. Difluprednate, a newer corticosteroid, may have a similar rate of elevation of IOP. Clinical studies suggest difluprednate has a similar adverse effect profile to prednisolone, but is associated with potentially higher rises in IOP.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What HLA typing result would best support a diagnosis of birdshot retinochoroidopathy?
pool.rationale: The HLA-A29 gene is strongly associated with birdshot retinochoroidopathy, with a sensitivity of 96% and a specificity of 93%. HLA-B27–associated ocular inflammatory conditions include anterior uveitis, scleritis, and peripheral ulcerative keratitis, but 5% to 10% of normal unaffected patients are carriers of this gene. HLA-DR4 and HLA-B51 each have statistically significant population associations with ocular inflammatory disease (DR4 with Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease and B51 with Behçet), but the modest positive and negative predictive values preclude meaningful use in most clinical scenarios.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 62-year-old patient with history of multiple surgeries to the right eye for penetrating trauma presents with bilateral granulomatous panuveitis responding to high-dose oral corticosteroids. What is the most likely mechanism of his inflammation?

options.c: loss of tolerance of intraocular antigens
options.d: loss of immunoregulatory systems of the anterior chamber

pool.rationale:
Sympathetic ophthalmia is thought to be due to loss of tolerance of intraocular antigens found in the uveal tract; a requirement for the diagnosis is previous trauma, intraocular surgery, or other disruption of the uveal tract.
HLA-B27-associated uveitis is usually anterior, episodic, and nongranulomatous, and onset of the first episode is typically earlier in life than in this patient. HLA-A29 is highly correlated with birdshot chorioretinopathy characterized by multiple yellow non-pigmented lesions at the level of the choroid, vitritis, and vasculitis. Loss of immunoregulatory systems of the anterior chamber plays a role in corneal graft rejection.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Gingival hyperplasia is a side effect of what immunosuppressive drug?
pool.rationale:
Cyclosporine induces gingival hyperplasia, and prophylactic dental cleaning and daily flossing are recommended for patients taking the drug.
Cyclophosphamide is associated with myelosuppression and hemorrhagic cystitis. Mycophenolate and methotrexate is associated with hepatotoxicity and gastrointestinal side effects.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common cause of hypotony after glaucoma surgery in a patient with uveitis?

options.c: ciliary body dysfunction resulting in decreased aqueous production
options.d: increased uveoscleral outflow due to increased permeability

pool.rationale: Intraocular surgery (including glaucoma surgery) in the setting of uveitis can lead to decreased aqueous production by the ciliary body and subsequent hypotony. Peripheral posterior synechiae (especially for 360 degrees) can lead to iris bombé with subsequent occlusion of the angle and elevated intraocular pressure. Uveoscleral outflow is typically increased by cycloplegics, adrenergic agonists, prostaglandin analogs, and cyclodialysis that can occur as a complication of surgery. Although cyclodialysis can be a cause of hypotony in any patient undergoing intraocular surgery, it is not the most common cause of hypotony in uveitic patients. Peripheral anterior synechiae can also occlude the angle, leading to ocular hypertension. Chronic corticosteroid use carries with it the risk of developing steroid-response ocular hypertension and glaucoma, not hypotony.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A new patient presents for a routine examination and has the finding shown (Fig 1). She states that she had an episode of eye redness, pain, and blurry vision a year ago when an eye doctor told her "you have high pressure and inflammation in the eye." What was the most likely cause of this episode?
pool.rationale:
The photo demonstrates an area of iris transillumination/iris atrophy and the description is consistent with a hypertensive uveitis. A hypertensive uveitis is very suggestive of a viral, namely herpetic, etiology. The features of segmental iris atrophy (which could be appreciated with retroillumination as transillumination defects) makes the case for a herpetic etiology even more convincing. Other findings can include KPs that extend above the cornea's equator and overlying corneal edema (representing an endotheliitis).
Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis is typically characterized not only by transient, recurrent bouts of hypertensive uveitis, but also iris heterochromia in the affected eye. The iris stromal atrophy is usually diffuse. Like many viral uveitides, Fuchs may have stellate keratic precipitates. Gonioscopy is important to perform in suspected cases because bridging vessels, abnormal vessels bridging the angle, may be seen.
Behçet uveitis is associated with hypopyon uveitis as well as retinitis and vasculitis. In severe anterior segment inflammation, iris bombé can develop, leading to angle-closure glaucoma.
Posner-Schlossman syndrome (PSS) is characterized by recurrent unilateral anterior uveitis with markedly elevated IOP. Corneal edema and KPs along with low-grade cell can also accompany these episodes. It is possibly associated with CMV, but males are more likely affected.
Neither Behçet nor PSS is typically associated with sectoral iris atrophy.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common intraocular infectious agent in AIDS patients?
pool.rationale:
CMV (cytomegalovirus) retinitis is the most common opportunistic ocular infection in patients with acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS). Other infectious agents that can affect the eye in patients with AIDS are herpes zoster virus (VZV), Toxoplasma gondii, Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Cryptococcus neoformans, Pneumocystis jiroveci, Candida species, Histoplasma capsulatum, molluscum contagiosum virus, microsporidia.
Acute retinal necrosis (ARN) is a kind of necrotizing herpetic retinopathy, seen in mostly in healthy adults; however, it has been reported in children and in immunocompromised patients, including those with AIDS. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based assays suggest that the most common cause of ARN is VZV, followed by HSV-1, HSV-2, and rarely CMV.

pool.q: What ophthalmic event is associated with the largest number of cases of sympathetic ophthalmia (SO)?

options.a: penetrating ocular injury with uveal loss

pool.rationale: SO is very rare, which limits the estimation of the true incidence of disease. Classically, it is thought to follow nonsurgical ocular trauma, with incidence up to 0.5%. More recently, however, ocular surgery, particularly vitreoretinal surgery, has surpassed trauma as the main risk for the development of SO.

pool.q: What complication of serpiginous choroiditis is suggested by the presence of subretinal fluid and hemorrhage?
pool.rationale:
Subretinal fluid and hemorrhage in a patient with serpiginous choroiditis is highly suspicious for choroidal neovascularization, a common and severe complication of this choroiditis.
Active choroiditis can present with retinal whitening or be associated with decreased visual acuity, but does not typically present with hemorrhage. Choroidal rupture may mimic choroidal neovascularization and present with subretinal fluid and hemorrhage. However, a supportive history or associated traumatic event would be expected. This would be uncommon in the elderly age group typically carrying the diagnosis of serpiginous choroiditis. Cystoid macular edema is rare with serpiginous choroiditis and would not present with subretinal fluid and hemorrhage.

pool.q: Among patients with cytomegalovirus retinitis (CMV) and AIDS, what effect would introducing highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) be expected to have on the incidence of associated complications?

options.a: The incidence of CMV retinitis and its associated complications would be reduced by about 80%.
options.b: The incidence of CMV retinitis and its associated complications would be reduced by about 30%.
options.c: The incidence of CMV retinitis and its associated complications would be increased by about 30%.
options.d: There would be no effect on the risk of retinal detachment.

pool.rationale: Prior to modern antiretroviral therapy, an estimated 30% of patients with HIV/AIDS, usually with CD4+ T lymphocyte counts ≤50 cells/μL, experienced CMV retinitis. Secondary to breaks in areas of peripheral retinal necrosis, rhegmatogenous retinal detachments occurred at a rate of approximately 33% per eye per year. Modern antiretroviral regimens have reduced the incidence of CMV retinitis and its associated complications, such as retinal detachment, by 80%. This decrease has stabilized, and new cases of CMV retinitis can occur in patients where combination antiretroviral treatment fails or in those who abandon treatment or experience immune reconstitution but do not develop CMV-specific immunity.

pool.q: A previously healthy 23-year-old patient has recurrent unilateral anterior uveitis, keratic precipitates, an IOP of 32 mm Hg, and 1+ cell and flare with mixed white and pigmented cells in the anterior chamber. The funduscopic exam is normal. Given the patient's appearance shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.d: human immunodeficiency virus-associated immune recovery uveitis

pool.rationale: The appearance of stellate keratic precipitates (KP) can be associated with several etiologies of ocular inflammation, including viral infections such as herpes simplex, herpes zoster, toxoplasmosis, and rubella virus (in the form of Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis). In a patient with recurrent iritis, elevated IOP, and stellate KP, the most likely diagnosis is herpes simplex infection. Iris atrophy with transillumination defects also is suggestive of infection with a member of the herpes virus family. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing and response to therapy can help confirm the diagnosis. Sarcoid uveitis is associated with large “mutton-fat” KPs and is usually bilateral. Pars planitis and toxoplasma retinochoroiditis may also present with stellate KP, but the diagnosis requires the presence of posterior segment findings. HIV immune recovery uveitis requires a previous low CD4 level with reconstitution following highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Pars planitis is a subset of intermediate uveitis with vitreous snowbanking or snowballs occurring in the absence of infectious or underlying systemic disease. Pars planitis can be associated with anterior chamber reaction; however, the funduscopic exam would reveal intermediate uveitis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: For the condition shown, what 2 entities would be the most likely causative organisms in an otherwise healthy 40-year-old man?

options.c: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium avium intracellulare

pool.rationale: The image illustrates acute retinal necrosis (ARN), also known as necrotizing herpetic retinitis. The 2 most common organisms responsible for this condition are herpes simplex and varicella-zoster viruses. Antiviral therapy is indicated for the treatment of this condition. Rubella is typically associated with a pigmentary retinopathy ("salt and pepper" appearance) from congenital infection and is one of the "TORCH" complexes. Rubeola rarely is associated with retinal pigmented epithelial clumping. Mycobacterium species are usually found in immunocompromised hosts, although ocular tuberculosis may affect the choroid in the setting of advanced (typically miliary) tuberculosis in a normal host. Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease) can very rarely cause a non-necrotic retinitis, but this is typically mild. Optic disc edema is more commonly the major feature of Lyme. Bartonella henselae (cat scratch fever) also typically causes disc edema.

pool.q: What is the typical pattern of chorioretinitis in West Nile virus?

options.a: linear groups of chorioretinal scars along the nerve fiber layer
options.b: large, flat placoid lesions at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium
options.c: optic nerve edema with star-shaped macular exudate
options.d: arteriolar attenuation and diffuse retinal pigment epithelial mottling

pool.rationale:
Ocular manifestations of West Nile virus include pain, photophobia, blurred vision, and conjunctival hyperemia. A characteristic multifocal chorioretinitis is present in most patients. The chorioretinal lesions vary in size and number and present in distinctive linear arrays following the course of retinal nerve fiber layer.
Fundoscopic examination in acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE) demonstrates large, flat, yellow-white placoid lesions at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium that are scattered throughout the posterior pole.
Neuroretinitis, characterized by vision loss, optic nerve swelling, and macular star formation, can be caused by Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch disease).
The fundus may initially appear normal in autoimmune retinopathy, but arteriolar attenuation, retinal pigment epithelial mottling, and diffuse retinal and optic nerve atrophy may develop as the disease progresses.

pool.q: A patient with HLA B27-related uveitis has poor vision related to cystoid macular edema despite control of anterior segment inflammation. What treatment should be tried?

options.a: intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) antibody injection

pool.rationale: Cystoid macular edema (CME) is a common cause of vision loss in eyes with uveitis. Treatment of CME must first be directed toward control of intraocular inflammation. If CME persists despite control of inflammation, periocular injection of corticosteroid may be used. Typically, 20-40 mg of triamcinolone is injected into the sub-Tenon space. Anti-VEGF therapies can also reduce inflammatory CME, but the action is short lived, and repeat injections are required. Topical NSAIDs can be beneficial in treating pseudophakic CME, but their effectiveness in treating uveitic CME is not established. Oral NSAIDs do not have a role in the treatment of CME.

pool.q: A sewer-system worker from Puerto Rico presents with uveitis-associated hypopyon. For what infection is this patient at particularly increased risk?
pool.rationale:
Although the natural reservoirs for Leptospira interrogans are animals, humans can become infected with this zoonotic organism, especially when their jobs place them in contact with an infected animal's urine. Thus, sewer workers, veterinarians, and farmers are at higher risk for this infection.  Interestingly, half of the cases identified in the US occur in Puerto Rico. Leptospirosis is distinguished from the other infectious agents listed here as often being characterized by hypopyon.
Tularemia (caused by Francisella tularensis) is acquired from the bites of ticks and deerflies, as well as from rabbits.
In brucellosis, contact with dogs, pigs, goats and meat, placentas, or milk from infected cows leads to acquiring Brucella. Meat packers, veterinarians, or farm hands would be the employees most affected.
Because the etiologic agent of onchocerciasis (river blindness) is the larva of Onchocerca volvulus, which is transmitted through the bite of a female black fly endemic to sub-Saharan Africa, a patient from that region would be most likely to have this parasitic infection.

pool.q: A 69-year-old woman who had cataract surgery 3 months ago has had several episodes of inflammation each time her topical corticosteroids have been tapered. She now has a hypopyon and an iris mass, necrotizing scleritis, and vitreous snowballs. What type of organism is most likely causative?
pool.rationale: Recurrent inflammation in an eye that has previously undergone surgery is concerning for chronic postoperative endophthalmitis. Chronic postoperative bacterial endophthalmitis is most commonly caused by Propionibacterium acnes, a gram-positive anaerobe. Other gram-positive bacteria, gram-negative bacteria, Mycobacterium species, and fungi, such as Candida parapsilosis, Aspergillus flavus, and Torulopsis candida, can also cause chronic postoperative endophthalmitis. While chronic postoperative fungal endophthalmitis may present similarly to a bacterial infection, certain clinical signs make a fungal etiology more likely, including a corneal infiltrate or edema, mass in the iris or ciliary body, necrotizing scleritis, vitreous snowballs, or a "string-of-pearls" appearance in the vitreous.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the etiology of multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis?
pool.rationale:
Multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis (MCP) is a condition characterized by intraocular inflammation and multifocal choroidal lesions occurring in the absence of a known ocular or systemic disease. The disease is typically bilateral and has a predilection for females in the second to sixth decades of life. The herpes simplex and Epstein-Barr viruses have been implicated in this disease process; however, a viral etiology has not been proven. Pathologic specimens obtained from eyes with MCP have shown variable findings, ranging from large numbers of B lymphocytes in the choroid to a predominance of T lymphocytes, suggesting that different immune mechanisms may produce a similar clinical picture, and that an initial viral infection may trigger an autoimmune process.
Treponema pallidum, Toxoplasma gondii, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis are organisms that can be associated with posterior uveitis, but are not the etiology of MCP.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with blurred vision and photopsias that started in her right eye, then affected her left eye also. She had a fever, malaise, and headache one week ago. Her fundus appearance is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.c: acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE)

pool.rationale:
Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE) occurs in otherwise healthy young adults, with men and women affected equally. Patients may have a viral prodrome. In rare cases, cerebrovasculitis can occur. Bilateral involvement is typical, with the fellow eye becoming involved days to weeks after the first eye. The characteristic examination finding is multifocal, flat gray-white lesions 1-2 disc areas in size involving the outer retina/retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).
MEWDS can also have a viral prodrome but is unilateral and characterized by small perifoveal spots and foveal granularity. Patients with AZOOR often have a normal retinal examination or mild RPE changes in the early stages and late pigment migration and focal perivenous sheathing. Serpiginous choroiditis is characterized by geographic peripapillary lesions with centrifugal extension.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What posterior uveitis disorder can present with marked visual symptoms but minimal findings on clinical exam?
pool.rationale: Acute zonal occult outer retinopathy (AZOOR) can present with numerous visual complaints but very minimal funduscopic changes; however, patients can have marked abnormalities on electroretinography (ERG), multifocal ERG, and visual field testing. The condition can even be misdiagnosed as functional vision loss if no additional testing is performed. Fundus pigment changes often appear in the later stages of the disease and can be more apparent on fluorescein angiography or fundus autofluorescence. Serpiginous choroiditis and PIC present with characteristic scars and foci of localized inflammation. Although the prodromal phase of Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome can have minimal ocular findings, patients have typical systemic symptoms and by the time they present with vision loss, they have panuveitis and exudative retinal detachments.

pool.q: What nonocular clinical feature is most common in patients with ocular Behçet disease (BD)?

options.a: positive human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B51 test result

pool.rationale: Oral ulcers are the most frequent clinical finding in BD, but any particular patient may manifest an array of signs and symptoms, including erythema nodosum (painful or recurrent, most commonly on the tibia and other extensor surfaces); cutaneous pathergy or pustule formation at the site of venipuncture; recurrent genital ulcers; or arthritis. Vasculitis and thrombophlebitis are less common. In some populations there is an association with HLA-B51, but this association lacks adequate predictive value for clinical use.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Toxocariasis is seen most commonly in what age group?
pool.rationale:
Children and young adults are affected disproportionately.
Ocular toxocariasis (OT) is a zoonotic infection caused by Toxocara canis and Toxocara cati. Dogs and cats, the definitive hosts of the roundworm, pass unembryonated eggs via their feces into the environment (often into the soil). According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), 30% of dogs younger than 6 months may deposit Toxocara eggs in their feces, and 25% of cats are infected with Toxocara cati. After 2–4 weeks, those eggs embryonate and become infectious. Transmission to humans occurs through ingestion of soil or contaminated food, or the fecal–oral route. Exposure to playgrounds, sandboxes, kittens, and puppies, as well as the pica eating disorder, are risk factors.
Rarely, humans may acquire the infection from undercooked meat. National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) data from 2011–2014 suggested an overall seroprevalence in the United States of 5.1%. In children, an increased rate of antibody positivity correlated to lack of health insurance. The prevalence was recently estimated to be 1% of a large uveitic population treated at tertiary care centers in northern California.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What important condition may mimic human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) uveitis?

options.c: idiopathic retinal vasculitis, aneurysms, and neuroretinitis (IRVAN)

pool.rationale: Human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1), a retrovirus of the Oncovirinae subfamily, is endemic in Japan, the Caribbean islands, and parts of Central and South America. The major target cell of HTLV-1 is the CD4+ T cell. HTLV-1 infection is the established cause of adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL), HTLV-1–associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paralysis (HAM/TSP), and HTLV-1 uveitis (HU), defined as uveitis of undetermined origin in an HTLV-1 carrier. HU is responsive to corticosteroid therapy. For cases that progress despite adequate therapy, the clinician must consider a masquerade syndrome, as both retinal infiltration caused by ATL and retinal degeneration associated with HAM/TSP have been shown to mimic HU.

pool.q: A patient presents with anterior scleritis as shown, weight loss, and a cough. What additional findings would be most specific for the diagnosis of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener granulomatosis)?

options.b: granulomatous inflammation of the lungs on chest radiograph

pool.rationale: The presence of C-ANCA antibodies in the serum is most specific for granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Granulomatous inflammation of the lung parenchyma is also supportive, but this may also be found in many infectious and inflammatory diseases. The ESR is a nonspecific marker of inflammation and can be used to follow the activity of systemic inflammatory diseases; however, it is not specific for any certain cause of inflammation. ANAs can be found in several other autoimmune disorders, such as lupus, but are also not specific for granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

pool.q: What condition can lead to elevated intraocular pressure due to blockage of the angle by inflammatory cells and debris?
pool.rationale:
Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis

Inflammatory open-angle glaucoma occurs when the trabecular meshwork is inflamed (trabeculitis) or blocked by inflammatory cells and debris, as commonly occurs with infectious causes of uveitis such as Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis, necrotizing herpetic retinitis. herpes simplex and varicella-zoster iridocyclitis. cytomegalovirus iridocyclitis (including the Posner-Schlossman type), sarcoid uveitis, and Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis (rubella-associated). This type of glaucoma usually responds to topical cycloplegics, corticosteroids, and specific treatment of the infectious agent. Chronic anterior segment inflammation may result in the formation of circumferential posterior synechiae, pupillary block, and iris bombé, resulting in subacute secondary peripheral angle closure. This condition occasionally occurs in patients with chronic granulomatous iridocyclitis associated with sarcoidosis or VKH syndrome and in those with recurrent nongranulomatous iridocyclitis, as is seen with ankylosing spondylitis. In patients with light-colored (blue, green, hazel) irides, peripheral iridotomy with the Nd:YAG or argon laser results in resolution of the bombé and angle closure if performed before permanent peripheral synechiae form. Acute secondary angle-closure glaucoma may occur when choroidal inflammation results in forward rotation of the ciliary body and lens-iris diaphragm. This can be the presenting sign of Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome or sympathetic ophthalmia. Patients present with pain, elevated lOP, no posterior synechiae, and severe inflammation. Ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) or ultrasound evaluation showing choroidal thickening and anterior rotation of the ciliary body is diagnostic. Treatment with aggressive corticosteroid therapy and aqueous suppressants is required.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most serious manifestation associated with acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE)?
pool.rationale:
Cerebral vasculitis can result in infarction in areas of the brain, which can eventually lead to stroke or death. Thus, cerebral vasculitis (which is a systemic condition associated with APMPPE) is the most serious manifestation of APMPPE.
Optic nerve edema in APMPPE resolves with resolution of the placoid lesions.
A viral prodrome can be ascertained upon review of a patient's history.
CNV can be seen rarely in APMPPE as well, but the condition is not as serious as cerebral vasculitis.

pool.q: In addition to a culture of the involved area, workup of infectious scleritis should include what diagnostic tests?

options.a: computed tomography imaging of the orbits
options.c: rheumatoid factor, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein
options.d: vitreal paracentesis with culture of fluid for bacteria

pool.rationale:
Infectious scleritis can occur after any ocular surgery, though pterygium surgery with beta irradiation or mitomycin C application, scleral buckling procedures, and penetrating trauma are well-known risk factors. When there is conjunctival erosion over an area of scleritis that is concerning for infection, culture of this area should be performed. Scleral biopsy may be indicated to allow for the acquisition of a greater amount of material with which to culture for bacteria, fungi, and, if indicated, viral culture or polymerase chain reaction. One should also evaluate for a noninfectious, autoinflammatory etiology as noninfectious scleritis can become secondarily infected if there is an overlying conjunctival defect. Thus, checking rheumatoid factor, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein is indicated.
A vitreal paracentesis with culture of the vitreous fluid will not be productive in an infectious scleritis, because the tissue that should be procured is the involved sclera itself. Pathergy testing has been used historically in evaluating patients with Behçet disease, but does not play a role in evaluating scleritis. Computed tomographic (CT) imaging of the orbits is not the most appropriate initial testing of the choices listed here. If there is concern for posterior scleral or choroidal involvement, B scan ultrasonography should be considered. Additionally, if there is concern for extension of a process into the orbit or perhaps originating in the sinuses, magnetic resonance imaging is superior to CT for visualizing soft tissues.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common side effect of mycophenolate mofetil?
pool.rationale: Gastrointestinal upset is the most common side effect of mycophenolate mofetil. Renal insufficiency is a side effect of cyclosporine and tacrolimus. Hirsutism is a side effect of cyclosporine. Headache is a nonspecific side effect.

pool.q: A 43-year-old woman presents with her second episode of acute anterior uveitis in her right eye, characterized by fine keratic precipitates, anterior chamber cells, and posterior synechiae without posterior segment involvement. This patient most likely has what systemic disease?
pool.rationale:
The patient has an acute anterior uveitis in her right eye, which is a classical presentation of reactive arthritis. Reactive arthritis is one of the seronegative spondyloarthropathies typically associated with the HLA-B27 major histocompatibility (MHC) class I surface antigen. The condition occurs most frequently in young adult men, although 10% of patients are women. A history of polyarthritis should be elicited upon review of systems.
Vitiligo is a dermatologic feature in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome; the uveitis in this condition is characterized early by bilateral choroiditis with areas of subretinal fluid and/or bullous serous retinal detachments.
Intraocular manifestations of systemic lupus erythematosus are characterized by vasculopathy (retinal vasculopathy with cotton-wool spots, intraretinal hemorrhages, or occlusive changes, as well as choroidopathy).
Rheumatoid arthritis typically presents as a scleritis and is the most common systemic illness associated with noninfectious scleritis. Sequelae associated with rheumatoid arthritis-associated scleritis can include uveitis, cataracts, glaucoma, posterior segment damage, and periph­eral ulcerative keratitis.

pool.q: In the setting of anterior uveitis, what finding is most specific for tubulointerstitial nephritis uveitis (TINU) syndrome?

options.d: presence of perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies

pool.rationale:
The findings in tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis (TINU) are abnormal serum creatinine and decreased creatinine clearance, increased urinary beta-2 microglobulin, proteinuria, pyuria, hematuria, and urinary white cell casts. There is a genetic susceptibility, and TINU has been reported to be strongly associated with HLA-DRB1*0102.
Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) had been linked to granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener granulomatosis), microscopic polyangiitis (MPA), and "renal-limited" vasculitis (pauci-immune glomerulonephritis without evidence of extrarenal disease).

pool.q: What systemic immunomodulatory therapy (IMT) can be given orally with weekly dosing and is considered first-line treatment for juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA)?
pool.rationale:
Methotrexate is an antimetabolite that is unique among immunosuppressive therapies in that it can be given orally or subcutaneously as a weekly dose. It is considered a first-line choice for IMT in children, and many studies have established its efficacy and safety in treatment of JIA patients.

Azathioprine is also an antimetabolite. It is given orally with daily dosing. Cyclosporine is a T-cell inhibitor that is also given orally with daily dosing. Infliximab is a tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha inhibitor that is administered with intravenous infusions.

pool.q: A patient with uveitis has urethritis and oral ulcers. Given the anterior and posterior findings shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: The anterior segment finding of posterior synechiae may be found in any of the uveitic conditions listed. However, the posterior segment finding of retinal vasculitis (sheathing of the vessels) that involves both arterioles and venules is consistent with Adamantiades-Behçet Disease (ABD). Additionally, the systemic findings of urethritis and oral ulcers are typical of the nonocular features of ABD. While syphilis can masquerade as a noninfectious uveitis, urethritis and oral ulcers are not typical for infection. Rather, a painless chancre at the site of inoculation (for example, genitalia) can be seen in primary syphilis. TINU can feature posterior synechiae, but retinal vasculitis is not seen. The nephritis seen in TINU is not characterized by urethritis. Instead, there can be white cell casts, protein, eosinophils, and blood found on urinalysis with microscopy. VKH does not feature urethritis or oral ulcers. Additionally, retinal vasculitis is not seen in VKH.

pool.q: A 22-year-old woman with bilateral panuveitis is being tested for tuberculosis (TB). She may have received bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination as a child. What test result would most likely indicate prior exposure to tuberculosis?

options.a: 10 mm of induration 48 hours after intracutaneous placement of purified protein derivative (PPD) 1 week after a reportedly negative skin test
options.b: positive result on interferon-based testing of peripheral blood lymphocytes
options.c: 6 mm of induration 48 hours after intracutaneous placement of purified protein derivative (PPD)

pool.rationale:
Previous immunization with BCG and intraluminal BCG treatment in bladder carcinoma can lead to false-positive skin test results with PPD testing.
Interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) are used for the diagnosis of latent or active tuberculosis infection. They indicate a cellular immune response to Mycobacterium. tuberculosis.
IGRAs are not affected by BCG vaccination status, so they are useful for evaluation of TB infection in BCG-vaccinated individuals.
Hilar adenopathy is not definitive for tuberculosis and can be seen in other diseases including sarcoidosis, which may cause panuveitis.

pool.q: What is an antibody?

options.a: a lipopolysaccharide that stimulates inflammatory mediators
options.b: a lymphocyte with specificity for non-self antigens
options.c: a glycoprotein able to bind to a specific molecular moiety
options.d: a serum protein produced in the thymus, with specificity for non-self antigens

pool.rationale: Antibodies are glycoproteins that are produced in lymph nodes and in areas of inflammation, which are specific for an antigen; they are produced by B lymphocytes that have been stimulated to mature into plasma cells after exposure to the appropriate antigen. The specificity of the antibody is determined by gene rearrangement of the B cell, and all of the antibodies produced are then identical and specific for the same antigen. Antibodies circulate in the serum and interstitial space, can be secreted in tears, and are found in other mucosal membranes.

pool.q: Based on epidemiologic data, what is the most common type of uveitis patient an ophthalmologist is likely to encounter?

options.a: a 26-year-old white man with a negative review of systems who presents with sudden-onset unilateral pain, redness, decreased vision, and photophobia
options.b: a 32-year-old white woman with multiple sclerosis (MS) who presents with subacute onset of floaters in both eyes
options.c: a 28-year-old Hispanic man with 3 cats at home who presents with sudden onset of floaters and worsening vision in his left eye
options.d: a 38-year-old woman of Native American descent who presents with sudden-onset floaters and decreased vision and, on examination, found to have bilateral exudative retinal detachments

pool.rationale:
Epidemiologically, the most common form of uveitis is anterior uveitis, followed by panuveitis, posterior uveitis, and lastly, intermediate uveitis. The patient with a negative review of systems who presents with sudden-onset unilateral pain, redness, decreased vision, and photophobia likely has HLA-B27-associated acute anterior uveitis. The patient with MS has intermediate uveitis secondary to her MS. The patient who has cats likely has posterior uveitis secondary to toxoplasmosis. The patient with bilateral exudative retinal detachments likely has panuveitis secondary to Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome.
(Aside: while HLA-B27 acute anterior uveitis is classically associated with one of the seronegative spondyloarthropathies [ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, enterohepatic arthritis, psoriatic arthritis] it is more common for a B27 (+) patient to present with acute anterior uveitis in the absence of any systemic manifestations, as opposed to first being diagnosed with one of the seronegative spondyloarthropathies and then presenting with acute anterior uveitis).

pool.q: What inflammatory cell type dominates the infiltrate in acute bacterial infections?
pool.rationale: Neutrophils are efficient phagocytes that readily clear tissues and degrade ingested material. They act as important effector cells through the release of granule products and cytokines. Neutrophils dominate the infiltrate in experimental models and clinical examples of active bacterial infections of the conjunctiva (conjunctivitis), sclera (scleritis), cornea (keratitis), and vitreous (endophthalmitis).

pool.q: In an immunocompromised patient, what is the most likely cause of the condition shown in the image below?
pool.rationale:
The fundus image shows opacification of the retina with areas of hemorrhage, exudate, and necrosis that are characteristic of CMV retinitis. CMV is a common ocular opportunistic infection in immunocompromised patients.
HSV and HZV cause acute retinal necrosis with large areas of retinal whitening and necrosis.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis typically causes choroiditis.

pool.q: Why might a patient with acute leptospirosis have resolution of systemic symptoms but continuing uveitis?

options.a: The eye and brain are immunologically privileged sites.
options.c: Residual antigens from the acute ocular infection trigger molecular mimicry, resulting in sterile inflammation.
options.d: There is an autoimmune component with relapsing symptoms mediated by immune complex deposition.

pool.rationale:
Leptospirosis is caused by a spirochetal bacterium commonly found in sewer water and rats. The majority of US cases occur in Hawaii. Because of its phylogenic similarity to other spirochetal bacteria such as Treponema pallidum, patients often have false-positive rapid plasma reagin (RPR) or fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) test results. If the systemic symptoms resolve but uveitis continues or recurs, persistence of leptospirosis in the eye, a privileged site, is the most likely cause.
A unique feature of the microenvironment of the eye is termed the ocular immune privilege. The term was introduced in 1940s by the finding that foreign antigen introduction to the anterior chamber did not elicit inflammatory response. Immune privilege is thought to be an evolutionary adaptation to protect vital structures. Traditionally, central nervous system, eyes, and testicles are considered immune-privileged organs.
Additional treatment with intravenous penicillin or oral tetracycline or doxycycline should be instituted. Although there can be immune manifestations of leptospirosis in the eye, this usually occurs after a prolonged interval after systemic disease, and would not be observed right after an acute phase.

pool.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with a history of photopsia of several months' duration. On examination there are no anterior chamber cells, keratic precipitates, or posterior synechiae. On examination after dilation, there is no vitritis, but there are several discrete lesions 100 μm to 200 μm diameter in the posterior segment. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
The patient described fits the typical patient with PIC: a young woman (18-40 years old) with photopsias. Other visual symptoms include paracentral scotomas and metamorphopsia. In multifocal choroiditis (MC), the lesions may range from 50 μm to 200 μm in size (and thus can be similar in size to PIC lesions), but there is an accompanying vitritis as often as anterior chamber cell. Additionally, the lesions in PIC typically do not extend out to the midperiphery, whereas in MC they can also be found peripherally. The creamy yellow/whitish lesions in birdshot range from 50 μm to 1500 μm in size and lie at the level of the choroid.
Patients with birdshot are typically middle-aged women (30-70 years of age). While this patient is of the appropriate gender for subretinal fibrosis and uveitis syndrome (nearly all patients are young women), the lesions, which occur at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium, are larger than those described by this patient, and the inflammation is also characterized by inflammation in the anterior chamber and vitreous.

pool.q: Within what layer or layers of the healthy conjunctiva are mast cells typically found?
pool.rationale: The conjunctival epithelium contains numerous goblet cells, Langerhans cells, and melanocytes. T lymphocytes are present in both the substantia propria and the epithelial layer. In healthy conjunctiva, mast cells are contained in the substantia propria. Once recruited by interleukin-5 and other mediators, mast cells migrate into the epithelium and are important in allergic immune reactions. The fibrous layer contains vessels, nerves, and the glands of Krause.

pool.q: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) in patients with uveitis is characterized by what feature?

options.a: a relatively high association with proliferative vitreoretinopathy
options.b: a relatively low association with panuveitis
options.c: a relatively high association with retinal dialysis
options.d: a relatively low association with infectious uveitis

pool.rationale: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment occurs in 3% of patients with uveitis. Panuveitis and infectious uveitis are the entities most commonly associated with RRD. Up to 30% of patients may have proliferative vitreoretinopathy at presentation. Retinal dialyses are more common in patients with RRD associated with trauma.

pool.q: Once the diagnosis of sympathetic ophthalmia is established, what is the preferred initial management?

options.a: intraocular injection of foscarnet to the sympathizing eye
options.c: panretinal laser photocoagulation to the sympathizing eye

pool.rationale:
In the rare instances when sympathetic ophthalmia does follow either injury or surgery, standard treatments such as corticosteroids almost always control the inflammation. Therefore, enucleation or evisceration of an injured eye to minimize risk of sympathetic ophthalmia should be undertaken only when the eye is painful, structurally disorganized, and has no light perception.
Panretinal photocoagulation has no place in managing this form of uveitis. Foscarnet is an antiviral antibiotic that is used to treat cytomegalovirus or other herpes viral retinitis, such as in acute retinal necrosis or as a complication of iatrogenic or infectious immunosuppression.

pool.q: A 3-month-old child with seizures who was born in an area noted to have mouse droppings is referred by the pediatric department for ophthalmologic examination. Abnormalities were noted on computed tomography (CT) scan and clinical examination. What antibody titer is most likely to be elevated in both mother and patient?
pool.rationale:
Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) is a fetal teratogen, passed vertically from mother to fetus during pregnancy. Rodents are the natural host and reservoir, and infection to the mother usually occurs after eating food contaminated with infected rodent excrement or by the bite of an infected rodent. The earlier in pregnancy a mother is infected, the more severe the sequelae in the developing fetus. Manifestations in a child born to a mother infected with LCMV during pregnancy include macrocephaly, hydrocephalus, periventricular calcifications with seizures, chorioretinal scars (very similar to toxoplasmosis scars), optic atrophy, nystagmus, and strabismus.
Toxoplasma gondii can present very similarly when transmitted to a fetus; however, the intracranial calcifications in congenital toxoplasmosis infection tend to be diffuse (as opposed to periventricular), and the natural hosts and reservoirs of Toxoplasma gondii are cats.
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection in a fetus can cause intracranial calcifications and hydrocephalus, but does not produce chorioretinal scarring.
Syphilis infection in a fetus does not typically produce intracranial calcifications or hydrocephalus, and again chorioretinal scarring is absent (syphilis infection can produce a diffuse, "salt-and-pepper" pigmentary retinopathy).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient with culture-positive Propionibacterium acnes infection after cataract surgery was treated with intravitreal antibiotics on 2 occasions. There is persistent intraocular inflammation. A repeat culture is positive again for P acnes. What is the next appropriate step?
pool.rationale:
Often there can be equatorial lens capsule sequestration of bacteria, which serves as a repository for chronic postoperative bacterial endophthalmitis caused by P acnes. In such a case, the requirement for repeat injections or pars plana vitrectomy with later recurrence of inflammation indicates that lens explantation is needed to eradicate the infection.
Administering topical, oral, and/or intravenous antibiotics is insufficient to treat bacterial endophthalmitis. Administering oral corticosteroids can help with inflammation initially, but it can also suppress the local immune system and allow the infection to progress unabated.

pool.q: How do MHC class I molecules differ structurally from MHC class II molecules?

options.a: MHC class I molecules express receptors for the Fc portion of immunoglobulin E, whereas MHC class II molecules do not.
options.b: Unlike MHC class II molecules, MHC class I molecules interact with CD4 T helper lymphocytes.
options.c: Unlike MHC class II molecules, MHC class I molecules are made up of 2 chains, with the second chain, the beta-2 microglobulin chain, being constant.
options.d: MHC class I molecules are composed of variable alpha and beta subunits, whereas class II molecules are composed of constant alpha and beta subunits.

pool.rationale: Both MHC class I and II molecules are heterodimers, being made up of alpha and beta chains. For both MHC class I and II molecules, the alpha subunits are encoded by the MHC gene. Additionally, the beta subunits for MHC class II molecules are also encoded by the MHC gene. The beta subunit for MHC class I molecules (specifically the beta-2 microglobulin subunit) is encoded by the beta-2 microglobulin gene and is not polymorphic (is constant across all MHC class I molecules).

pool.q: A 39-year-old asymptomatic woman with no past medical history undergoes routine funduscopic examination. The only abnormality seen is cotton-wool spots. Blood pressure is normal in the clinic. Based on the clinical examination, what finding is most likely?
pool.rationale:
The question stem describes HIV retinopathy, which can appear very similar to hypertensive retinopathy (cotton-wool spots, intraretinal hemorrhages, attenuated vessels, etc.). A low CD4+ cell count is the only finding among the answer choices listed that identifies a patient with HIV infection.
There is no reason for this patient to have diminished color vision. There is no mention of vessel tortuosity, attenuation, or arteriovenous nicking to suggest impending CRVO. Lastly, CMV retinitis, which can occur in patients with HIV infection, typically occurs with CD4+ cell counts below 50 cells/μL and typically manifests as focal areas of ischemic retina and edema with overlying hemorrhages.

pool.q: What is the most common disorder associated with human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B27 acute anterior uveitis?
pool.rationale:
Among patients with HLA-B27-associated anterior uveitis, ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is the most common associated systemic manifestation (about 90% of patients with AS are HLA-B27+). Conversely, patients with AS are also the group most likely to develop acute anterior uveitis. However, most patients who test positive for the HLA-B27 antigen do not develop AS.
Behçet disease is typically sporadic and not associated with HLA-B27.
Systemic lupus erythematosus is an uncommon cause of anterior uveitis, and neither SLE nor toxoplasmosis is related to the HLA-B27 antigen. Host genetic factors may be related to the development of recurrent toxoplasmosis, but these factors are not yet well-defined.

pool.q: A 9-year-old child presents with neuroretinitis. What test will most likely lead to a specific diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Bartonella titers

Cats are the primary reservoir of Bartonella henselae, an infectious cause of neuroretinitis in humans. The frequency of seropositivity in the North American population is low, lending a higher positive predictive value to positive serum titers in the setting of neuroretinitis. In contrast, CMV seropositivity is much more common, and not typically associated with neuroretinitis; CMV more commonly causes retinitis or anterior uveitis.
Angiotensin-converting enzyme levels may be elevated in many diseases that involve the lungs, including sarcoidosis, but are less specific in children.
The erythrocyte sedimentation rate is very nonspecific, and may be abnormal in a broad range of infectious, inflammatory, and neoplastic conditions.

pool.q: Onchocerciasis is caused by the filarial parasite Onchocerca volvulus. What is the vector of transmission?
pool.rationale: Onchocerca volvulus larvae are transmitted from the bite of a female black fly (Simulium genus) to humans, causing onchocerciasis, or river blindness (the black flies breed near fast-flowing rivers). Female sandflies transmit Leishmania (responsible for causing leishmaniasis). Female Anopheles mosquitos transmit Plasmodium falciparum, which causes malaria. Tsetse flies (genus Glossina) transmit Trypanosoma brucei, a protozoan that causes trypanosomiasis, or sleeping sickness.
