pool.q: What immunologic mechanism is most important in the response to mycobacteria infections such as tuberculosis?

options.a: serum interferon alpha levels inducing cytotoxicity
options.b: conversion of macrophages to giant cells that form caseating granulomas
options.c: B cell co-stimulation of T cells
options.d: B cell activation which results in immunoglobulin G production

pool.rationale: Tissue macrophages ingest mycobacteria bacilli, but are unable to eradicate them. Activated T cells induce, via cytokines, conversion of the macrophages into multinucleated giant cells that can more effectively contain the infection. However, viable organisms may persist, allowing reactivation of infection even decades after exposure. This risk is elevated with immunosuppression, especially with a tumor necrosis factor-alpha inhibitor medication, such as infliximab. Memory T cells provide the delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction that results in the tuberculin skin test (purified protein derivative test). Antibody production by B-cells does not contribute significantly to the immune response to tuberculosis, and serum interferon-alpha is also not a significant aspect of immunity to this organism. B cells may act as antigen presenting cells, but Mycobacterium is an intracellular pathogen that persists inside phagocytic immune cells, minimizing the effectiveness of extracellular immune surveillance.

pool.q: A patient with chronic bilateral anterior uveitis has a negative serum Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) and a weakly positive (1+ on a 1-4+ scale) fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) test result. What test would be the most appropriate next step?

options.c: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the brain
options.d: serum microhemagglutination assay for T pallidum (MHA-TP)

pool.rationale:
T pallidum (MHA-TP)

False positives are possible with the FTA-ABS test. It is read by technicians and 1+ is at best very weakly positive (thus, FTA-ABS is a qualitative test). The ophthalmologist could repeat the FTA-ABS test or consider a lumbar puncture to obtain cerebrospinal fluid for VDRL testing. A second serologic treponemal antigen test, such as a microhemagglutination assay (MHA-TP) could be performed in this case.
Consideration for serologic testing can be given to a nonspecific test (nontreponemal antigen test) like the RPR, but this type of test will not change the need for specific antitreponemal serologies, because these tests can be negative in ocular/neuro syphilis or in latent syphilis.
An ACE test is considered when sarcoidosis is in the differential diagnosis for uveitis. No specific findings of ocular syphilis can be yielded by a brain MRI.

pool.q: The term candlewax drippings describes what ocular findings associated with sarcoidosis?

options.a: corneal endothelial deposits of inflammatory cells
options.b: clumps of cells in the anterior vitreous
options.c: iris nodules at the pupillary margin

pool.rationale: Ocular manifestations of sarcoidosis are numerous and protean. However, the most common manifestations include granulomatous anterior uveitis with mutton fat keratic precipitates, iris nodules, and retinal periphlebitis. "Taches de bougie," also known as "candlewax drippings," is a description of irregular granulomas along retinal venules, which have been likened to dried wax drippings on candles.

pool.q: What type of glaucoma management is contraindicated in patients with uveitis?
pool.rationale:
Uveitic glaucoma can lead to optic nerve damage and further visual loss unless adequately controlled. Medical management includes all topical anti-glaucoma drops (with prostaglandin analogs such as latanoprost, travoprost, bimatoprost), as well systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitors. Some argue that prostaglandin analogues should be avoided in all cases of uveitis, although there is some debate on this subject.
If medical management of glaucoma fails, glaucoma filtering surgery, aqueous drainage devices (eg, Ahmed valve, Baerveldt implant) are indicated. Laser trabeculoplasty should be avoided in uveitic eyes as it may exacerbate inflammation. In addition, laser trabeculoplasty is often ineffective in uveitic eyes.

pool.q: Delayed endophthalmitis (> 6 weeks) following cataract surgery is commonly caused by what pathogen?
pool.rationale:
Propionibacterium acnes

Propionibacterium acnes is well known to cause a delayed or chronic mild endophthalmitis, following cataract or neodymium yttrium-argon-garnet (Nd:YAG) laser surgery, that can be confused with a noninfectious uveitis. Often no hypopyon or pain is present. The lens capsule may show gray-white deposits indicative of P acnes growth. 
Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Bacillus cereus usually present acutely with typical signs of exogenous bacterial endophthalmitis such as pain, cells and flare, hypopyon, and decreased vision.

pool.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with her first episode of dull eye pain with 2+ diffuse injection that does not blanch with topical phenylephrine. She reports no other ocular or systemic symptoms. On examination there is no necrosis, and B-scan is within normal limits. What major systemic side effect is associated with use of the standard first-line medication for her inflammation?
pool.rationale:
This patient presents with the classic symptom and signs for scleritis with the dull aching pain, and injection that does not resolve with the instillation of a topical vasoconstrictor (phenylephrine), indicating the injection is deeper in the sclera (only vessels as deep as the episcleral vessels will blanch with topical vasoconstrictors). Since this is her first episode and it is mild-moderate, the first-line or primary treatment would be a few weeks of oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen, naproxen, or indomethacin, if there are no contraindications. Topical therapy is generally not sufficient for scleritis. When starting oral NSAIDs, the patient should be counseled on the increased risk for stomach or intestinal ulcers, which can be life-threatening if severe. Initiating concomitant histamine-H2 receptor antagonists or proton-pump inhibitors may help reduce the risk of gastroduodenal ulceration. Renal function should also be closely monitored.
Hepatotoxicity, malignancy, and hyperglycemia are adverse effects of treatments for severe or refractory noninfectious scleritis and are not seen with use of NSAIDs. The following treatments should not be used for infectious scleritis.
Immunomodulatory therapy (IMT) is used to treat scleritis; however, it is used only after NSAIDs and steroids have failed. One commonly used class of nonbiologic IMT is antimetabolites. Methotrexate is a folic acid analogue and dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor that exerts anti-inflammatory effects via extracellular release of adenosine. It is associated with reversible hepatotoxicity in up to 15% of patients. Azathioprine is another antimetabolite, a purine nucleoside analogue that disrupts DNA replication and RNA transcription, can also cause reversible mild hepatotoxicity. Because this case is in the mild-moderate category and has not proven to be refractory, an immunomodulatory treatment would not be indicated yet before NSAIDs.
Another class of IMT is alkylating agents, which are used only if other IMTs fail to control the scleritis. The most concerning adverse effect of these medications, such as cyclophosphamide and chlorambucil, is the increased malignancy risk. Thus, use of these is limited, and only warranted for severe, vision- or life-threatening inflammation, which this patient does not have at this time. As a side note, alkylating agents may be used as first-line treatment for necrotizing scleritis in the setting of systemic vasculitides, including granulomatosis with polyangiitis or relapsing polychondritis.
Systemic steroids are reserved for scleritis cases refractory to NSAIDs, or severe cases with posterior or necrotizing presentations, which this patient does not have; she has a normal B-scan (no T-sign) and no necrosis (thinning of sclera with uveal show). Initial dosing of prednisone or the equivalent is 1 mg/kg/day, followed by a slow taper. Hyperglycemia can present with short-term use of steroids, and diabetes mellitus can develop with intermediate or longer-term use. Systemic steroid can also exacerbate peptic ulcers or gastric reflux; thus, if a patient is taking both NSAIDs and steroids, a histamine-H2 receptor antagonist or a proton-pump inhibitor should be initiated.
Review of side effects of systemic steroids
Short-term risks:
  • ocular hypertension
  • hyperglycemia
  • systemic hypertension
  • gastric reflux
  • insomnia
  • emotional lability
  • weight gain
  • fluid retention
Intermediate-term risks:
  • cataract
  • osteoporosis
  • avascular necrosis of joints
  • diabetes mellitus
The patient's general health should be monitored while she is on steroids, and assistance of an internist may be required.

pool.q: In evaluating a patient with chronic uveitis for syphilis, what test is least specific due to its high false-positive rate for a variety of conditions?

options.a: cerebral spinal fluid for cytology, cell counts, and Venereal Disease Research laboratory (VDRL)
options.b: serum microhemagglutination assay for Treponema pallidum (MHA-TP)

pool.rationale:
Nontreponemal serum tests, such as serum VDRL and RPR, may be falsely elevated in several systemic conditions other than syphilis, including lupus erythematosus, leprosy, advanced age, intravenous drug abuse, bacterial endocarditis, tuberculosis (TB), vaccinations, infectious mononucleosis, HIV infection, pregnancy, atypical pneumonia, malaria, rickettsial infections, and other spirochetal infections. Additionally, nontreponemal serum tests may become negative in up to 30% of patients with late, untreated syphilis. As such, serum RPR alone is the least helpful in diagnosing a patient suspected of having syphilitic uveitis. Nontreponemal cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tests are much more likely to remain positive in untreated disease, and the only nontreponemal test that should be performed on CSF samples is VDRL.
Treponemal tests, such as FTA-ABS and MHA-TP, remain positive for the life of the patient infected with syphilis and are used to confirm positive nontreponemal tests.

pool.q: A 22-year-old man presents with worsening vision, redness, and pain in his right eye. He sustained trauma with a self-sealing corneal laceration 2 weeks ago. His vision is now light perception (LP) OD and 20/20 OS, with intraocular pressures of 66 OD and 14 OS. In addition to a mature cataract, 3+ anterior chamber and vitreous cell is noted OD, as well as the following corneal pathology. The left eye examination is unremarkable. What is the most likely explanation for his elevated intraocular pressure?
pool.rationale:
There are several "lens-induced" glaucomas; 3 are secondary open-angle (phacoantigenic [previously termed phacoanaphylactic], phacolytic, lens-particle), and 1 is secondary angle-closure (phacomorphic).
Phacoantigenic uveitis is a form of uveitis that develops when a patient is sensitized to his or her own lens protein. It often occurs in a posttraumatic setting, with disruption of the lens capsule. Since the immune sensitization does not involve immunoglobulin E (IgE), the stem “anaphylaxis” of the older term, phacoanaphylactic, is confusing. The presentation of phacoantigenic uveitis is of a granulomatous uveitis (ie, large, “greasy" or "mutton-fat” keratic precipitates, iris nodules). In this vignette, the mature cataract and keratic precipitates are suggestive of violation of the lens capsule and associated phacoantigenic uveitis.
Phacolytic uveitis, also termed phacolytic glaucoma, is a complication of a mature or hypermature (liquefied) cataract that results in the leaking of lens proteins through an intact lens capsule. Typical findings include cells, flare, and lens-engorged macrophages settled in the inferior trabecular meshwork. In contrast to phacoantigenic/phacoanaphylactic uveitis, there are usually no keratic precipitates or synechiae present.
Lens particle glaucoma results from fragments of cortical lens obstructing the trabecular meshwork.
In phacomorphic glaucoma, an enlarging or intumescent cataract grows in the anterior-posterior dimension and thus pushes the iris forward, leading to angle closure.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What ocular inflammatory disease is characterized by unilateral stellate keratic precipitates, cataract development, and increased risk of glaucoma?
pool.rationale: Fuchs heterochromic uveitis (also sometimes called Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis or Fuchs uveitis syndrome) is characterized by chronic low-grade anterior chamber inflammation, diffuse stellate keratic precipitates (rather than the inferior distribution in Arlt triangle seen in other causes of anterior uveitis), elevated IOP, diffuse iris atrophy with transillumination defects, and cataract development. Approximately 5% of cases can be bilateral, and there is evidence that rubella infection is the etiology. HLA-B27-associated uveitis is typically episodic, and associated with nongranulomatous inflammation that can be fibrinous and lead to hypopyon development; however, stellate keratic precipitates and elevated pressure are not typical. Sympathetic ophthalmia is classically granulomatous, and juvenile xanthogranuloma is a common cause of spontaneous hyphema, rather than true intraocular inflammation.

pool.q: What is the preferred treatment for the acute phase of serpiginous choroidopathy?

options.d: intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy

pool.rationale:
Serpiginous choroidopathy is a typically bilateral, chronic, progressive, recurrent inflammatory disease of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), choriocapillaris, and choroid; the etiology of the condition is undetermined. Local and systemic corticosteroids are the preferred therapies for the acute phase of the disorder. Demonstrating a high rate of recurrence, serpiginous choroidopathy usually requires long-term anti-inflammatory treatment with steroid-sparing agents, such as cyclosporine A and/or azathioprine.
As a definite viral etiology of serpiginous choroidopathy has not been proven, antiviral therapy is not indicated. Although intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy may be beneficial when serpiginous choroidopathy is complicated by choroidal neovascularization (CNV), it is not been shown to be an effective therapy for serpiginous choroidopathy itself.

pool.q: A patient presents with chronic intraocular inflammation 4 months after uncomplicated cataract surgery with intraocular lens implantation. The patient had no inflammation prior to surgery. Examination discloses keratic precipitates, 1+ anterior chamber and 1+ vitreous cell. An intravitreal injection of 1 mg of vancomycin does not resolve the inflammation. What intervention is recommended?

options.b: intravitreal injection of 2 mg of triamcinolone
options.c: vitreous biopsy for flow cytometry and histopathology
options.d: removal of lens and capsular bag with repeated antibiotic injection

pool.rationale: Chronic postoperative endophthalmitis presents with recurrent bouts of indolent inflammation in an eye with previous history of ocular surgery, most commonly cataract surgery. Intravitreal corticosteroid injection should not be employed unless infectious endophthalmitis is ruled out. Chronic postoperative bacterial endophthalmitis is most commonly caused by Propionibacterium acnes (P acnes). Staphylococcus epidermis and Corynebacterium species can cause chronic postoperative endophthalmitis, too. P acnes may sequester itself between the intraocular lens (IOL) and the posterior capsule. This may present as whitish plaques. In such cases, intravitreal vancomycin is not curative; IOL explantation and complete capsulectomy, in addition to intravitreal vancomycin injection, should be performed. The specimens should be sent for stain, culture, and sensitivity.

pool.q: When given as long-term therapy for noninfectious uveitis, what systemic drug would have the lowest risk of toxicity?
pool.rationale:
When long-term therapy is needed for the management of uveitis, systemic immunomodulatory therapy has, in general, fewer overall side effects than chronic use of systemic prednisone. The antimetabolites (including methotrexate and mycophenolate) are frequently employed as first-line therapy for corticosteroid-sparing control of uveitis. Of the medications listed, methotrexate has the lowest risk of overall toxicity. Hepatoxicity (which can be monitored by checking liver function tests regularly) can occur with methotrexate. By contrast, the side effects of prednisone include psychological disturbances, hypertension, gastric ulcers, osteoporosis, femoral head osteonecrosis, and elevated serum glucose levels.
Cyclophosphamide and chlorambucil are both alkylating agents. As such, cyclophosphamide can cause hemorrhagic cystitis, myelosuppression, teratogenicity, sterility, and opportunistic infections. Chlorambucil is associated with teratogenicity, myelosuppression, and sterility.

pool.q: What is the most common cause of decreased vision in patients with uveitis?
pool.rationale:
Uveitic macular edema is the most common cause of vision loss in eyes with uveitis.
Uveitic glaucoma can develop from a combination of mechanisms, including from treatment with steroid medications.
Choroidal neovascularization can develop in uveitis due to disruption of the Bruch membrane from choroidal inflammation and the presence of inflammatory cytokines that promote angiogenesis.
Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment occurs in 3% of patients with uveitis and is most commonly associated with panuveitis and infectious uveitis.

pool.q: What infectious uveitic disorder may closely mimic acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE)?
pool.rationale:
The placoid lesions in APMPPE occur at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and underlying choroid. Similar lesions can be a presentation in syphilitic chorioretinitis, and checking rapid plasma reagin (RPR) and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption (FTA-ABS) is an important part of the diagnostic evaluation of APMPPE (see Table).
West Nile virus will appear as discrete punctate chorioretinal lesions that follow the retinal nerve fiber layer in a linear fashion.
Herpetic uveitis can be varied in its presentation, from a granulomatous anterior uveitis to posterior retinitis, depending on whether HSV or VZV is the etiology. Acute retinal necrosis (ARN) can occur with either of these pathogens and may present as a panuveitis or a viral retinitis, even leading to retinal detachments.
Toxoplasma gondii uveitis can present with many different findings as well, depending on whether it is congenital or acquired. Acquired disease classically presents with a focal white retinochoroiditis with overlying vitreous inflammation ("headlight in the fog"), often adjacent to a chorioretinal scar.

pool.q: What therapy would be contraindicated in a patient with multiple sclerosis-associated uveitis?
pool.rationale:
TNF-alpha inhibitors have been implicated in the appearance of demyelinating lesions. As such, these agents should be avoided in patients with MS to avoid exacerbation of their underlying demyelinating disease.
Furthermore, it is important to consider the possibility of MS in patients presenting with intermediate uveitis or pars planitis when contemplating treatment with anti-TNF-alpha agents that may exacerbate demyelination in MS.
Corticosteroids and antimetabolites are used in treating relapses of MS.

pool.q: What mediator plays a role in anterior chamber–associated immune deviation (ACAID)?
pool.rationale: Transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta) and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) play roles as regulators of ACAID. Interferon gamma causes neutrophil and macrophage infiltration. Substance P plays a role in vascular permeability and causes leukocyte infiltration. Tumor necrosis factor-alpha is involved in mononuclear cell infiltration.

pool.q: Uveitis develops most commonly in what stage of syphilis?
pool.rationale:
Uveitis may occur in any stage of syphilis but is seen most commonly (10% of cases) in secondary syphilis.
Tertiary syphilis is associated with uveitis in about 5% of cases.

pool.q: What is the most common ocular manifestation associated with inflammatory bowel disease?
pool.rationale: Patients with inflammatory bowel disease are at risk for anterior uveitis and less commonly scleritis, retinal vasculitis, keratitis, or orbital inflammation. Often the patients who develop uveitis also carry the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) B27 genotype. Primary open-angle glaucoma, retinal necrosis, and retinoschisis are not related to inflammatory bowel disease, although secondary glaucoma may develop in patients with ocular inflammation.

pool.q: What treatment is likely to resolve human T-lymphotropic virus type -1 (HTLV-1) -associated retinal vasculitis?
pool.rationale:
Human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) is a retrovirus endemic to Japan, the Caribbean Islands, and Central and South America. About 1% of uveitis cases in Japan are due to HTLV-1.
HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATL), HTLV-1-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paralysis (HAM/TSP), and HTLV-1 uveitis. Most cases of HTLV-1 uveitis (HU) are classified as intermediate uveitis (75%). Patients also present with keratopathy, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, mild granulomatous uveitis, unilateral vitritis, membranous vitreous opacities, and "snowballs." Retinal vasculitis, exudative retinal lesions, optic nerve abnormalities, and cystoid macular edema may be seen. HU is an inflammatory condition, probably due to inflammatory cytokines released by HTLV-1-infected CD4+ T cells, so retinal vasculitis is very responsive to systemic corticosteroids.
Individuals infected with HTLV-1 are at risk for other opportunistic infections, as HTLV-1 alters the host immune response, so other infectious etiologies including HIV, syphilis, and cytomegalovirus (CMV) should be considered in HTLV-1 carriers.
Zidovudine is used in human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), (formerly termed HTLV III), infection.
Intravitreal methotrexate is used for ocular involvement with primary central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma.
Lamivudine is noted to have mixed in vitro and in vivo benefits in HTLV-1 infection, despite an apparent absence of antiviral activity. It is not indicated in retinal vasculitis associated with HTLV-1.

pool.q: Among the white dot syndromes, for what disorder are the lesions on fluorescein angiography (FA) least apparent?

options.c: acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy

pool.rationale:
FA in birdshot uveitis reveals inconsistent findings depending on the age of the lesions and the phase of the study. Early birdshot uveitis lesions can show initial hypofluorescence with subtle late staining. In general, however, FA does not typically highlight the lesions themselves, but rather is useful in identifying more subtle types of active inflammation such as retinal vasculitis, cystoid macular edema, and optic nerve head leakage.
In contrast, in patients with acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE), FA shows characteristic early blockage with late staining of the lesions, and in patients with punctate inner choroiditis (PIC), it reveals early hyperfluorescence with late staining of the lesions. In patients with serpiginous choroiditis, FA reveals blockage of the choroidal flush in the early stage of the study and staining of the active edge of the lesion in the later stage. Early hyperfluorescence with late leakage is indicative of choroidal neovascular membranes, which are observed frequently in patients with PIC and less often in those with serpiginous choroiditis or birdshot uveitis.

pool.q: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA)–associated uveitis occurs most commonly in oligoarticular-onset JIA, and a subset typically affects girls who test positive for ANA. What should the treatment strategy include?

options.a: early consideration of systemic IMT such as with methotrexate
options.b: intravitreal corticosteroids repeated periodically based on the level of disease activity
options.c: topical corticosteroids and cycloplegics only, at whatever dose is required for as long as required, avoiding systemic IMT in children
options.d: long-term therapy with oral corticosteroids to control inflammation as the mainstay of therapy

pool.rationale: The main goals of therapy in the treatment of JIA-associated uveitis are the elimination of active intraocular inflammation, preservation of vision, and prevention of new structural complications such as posterior synechiae, cataract formation, and development of macular edema. Because the long-term use of both oral and topical corticosteroids typically leads to significant complications in children, it is important to consider systemic IMT early in the disease course.

pool.q: What is the tissue-equivalent immune cell of the basophil?
pool.rationale:
Basophils are the blood-borne equivalent of the tissue-bound mast cell. Once basophils leave the bloodstream and take residence in tissue, they become mast cells. The other answer choices (macrophage, dendritic cell, Langerhans cell) are incorrect pairings of blood- and tissue-equivalent cells.
Monocytes are the blood-borne equivalent of tissue-bound macrophages. Blood dendritic cells are precursors of tissue and lymphoid organ dendritic cells (they are not given a different name). Eosinophils are not given a different name in tissue.

pool.q: What would be an anticipated intraoperative complication in a 40-year-old man with Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis?
pool.rationale:
Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis (also termed Fuchs uveitis syndrome or Fuchs heterochromic uveitis) is characterized by unilateral, diffuse, small, white, stellate keratic precipitates; cells in the anterior chamber and the anterior vitreous; and heterochromia due to diffuse iris stromal atrophy. It is thought to be associated with viral infections (cytomegalovirus [CMV], rubella) and in other cases with toxoplasmosis. Glaucoma and cataracts occur frequently. Aqueous misdirection is a rare complication. Abnormal bridging vessels may be present in the iridocorneal angle. These may bleed during the cataract surgery and may lead to hyphema (this bleeding occurrence is known as Amsler sign [or Amsler-Verrey sign]).
Corneal edema is associated with Fuchs corneal dystrophy, not Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis.

pool.q: A 70-year-old man with no prior ocular history presents with 0.5+ anterior chamber cells and 2+ anterior chamber flare. Intraocular pressure is 10 mm Hg. Dilated funduscopy of the affected eye shows arteriolar narrowing and tortuous venules. What is the best test to perform to help with the diagnosis of this patient's condition?

options.b: chorioretinal biopsy with histopathology directed for a B-cell lymphoma
options.c: fundus autofluorescence to evaluate for peripapillary hyperautofluorescence
options.d: anterior chamber paracentesis with polymerase chain reaction testing for cytomegalovirus

pool.rationale: The case described is most consistent with ocular ischemic syndrome, which may feature anterior chamber inflammation, often with more prominent flare compared to anterior chamber cells. Thus, carotid ultrasonography will be the most helpful for making a diagnosis of clinically suspected ocular ischemic syndrome. Cytomegalovirus-associated anterior uveitis often features diffuse keratic precipitates and frequently is associated with ocular hypertension. A chorioretinal biopsy evaluating for a B-cell lymphoma (primary vitreoretinal lymphoma) is not indicated, as there are no subretinal lesions noted. Fundus autofluorescence will not be helpful in identifying the etiology of this patient's inflammation. Peripapillary hyperautofluorescence can be seen in some uveitic entities, including acute zonal occult outer retinopathy and acute idiopathic blind spot enlargement.

pool.q: A 27-year-old patient presents with panuveitis. The history and physical examination do not clearly indicate the cause of the uveitis. What test is appropriate to order?

options.a: liver function tests, complete blood cell (CBC) count, and brain imaging
options.b: antinuclear antibody testing, HLA typing, and sacroiliac joint imaging
options.c: creatinine analysis, urine analysis, and abdomen imaging
options.d: purified protein derivative skin test, syphilis serologies, and chest imaging

pool.rationale: When the history and physical examination do not clearly indicate the cause of the uveitis, tuberculosis, syphilis, and sarcoidosis should be ruled out as common causes of uveitis. HLA typing and sacroiliac joint imaging are ordered when seronegative spondyloarthropathy is suspected on history and physical examination. CBC and liver function tests are ordered when immune modulatory therapy is considered. Creatinine and urine analysis are ordered when glomerulonephritis is suspected.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is a symptom of anterior uveitis, but not a symptom of posterior uveitis?
pool.rationale: Photophobia is a symptom specific to the anterior segment of the eye and is typically due to inflammation of the iris and/or ciliary spasm, but it is not described by patients who exhibit posterior uveitis. Floaters can occur in intermediate and posterior uveitides, transient photopsias often reflect retinal involvement, and decreased vision can be seen in both anterior and posterior uveitis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient with a long history of anterior uveitis wishes to have cataract surgery. What is a prerequisite for any elective intraocular surgery in uveitic eyes?

options.c: adequate view of the posterior segment

pool.rationale: Any eye with chronic or recurrent uveitis may develop a cataract as a result of the inflammation or the corticosteroids used for treatment. Indications for cataract surgery in uveitic eyes are the same as for all cataracts: when the cataract causes functional impairment that interferes with activities of daily living; when the cataract is responsible for at least a portion of that visual decrease; and when functional improvement is likely to occur after cataract extraction. There is no prerequisite visual acuity. Additional considerations for cataract surgery in uveitic eyes are whether a cataract precludes the clinician from obtaining an adequate view of the fundus—thereby inhibiting appropriate monitoring of posterior segment disease or health. An adequate view of the posterior segment is therefore not a requirement. Uveitic eyes are at greater risk for postoperative complications than nonuveitic eyes. Thus, careful planning for surgery, including preoperative medical management and the timing of the procedure, is of utmost importance. The key to a successful visual outcome is meticulous long-term control of inflammation before proceeding with surgery. This may require immunomodulatory therapy in some patients, but is not a required treatment before cataract surgery. Common advice is to achieve the best control possible without flare-ups for at least 3 months prior to cataract surgery.

pool.q: What further testing may be required in a patient with nongranulomatous anterior uveitis with hypopyon and HLA-B27-positive ankylosing spondylitis?

options.a: aqueous tap for polymerase chain reaction testing

pool.rationale:
Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) may range in severity from asymptomatic to severe, crippling disease. Up to 90% of patients with AS test positive for HLA-B27. About 25% of HLA-B27-positive patients will develop spondyloarthritis or eye disease. Sacroiliac imaging studies should be obtained when indicated by a suggestive history. Patients should be informed of the risk of deformity and referred to a rheumatologist. Pulmonary apical fibrosis and cardiovascular disease (aortic valvular insufficiency) may also develop, so if the patient is symptomatic, it may be worthwhile to do chest imaging or cardiac echogram to rule these out.
Although these patients may present with hypopyon, this is usually sterile, so aqueous tap is not indicated unless for research purposes. Pathergy is a skin condition in which a minor trauma such as a bump or bruise leads to the development of skin lesions or ulcers that may be resistant to healing. Pathergy is seen with both Behçet disease and pyoderma gangrenosum. Urinalysis is usually not indicated in patients with ankylosing spondylitis.

pool.q: A definitive diagnosis of diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN) is most strongly supported by the results of what evaluation?

options.c: retinal examination with observation of the parasite in the subretinal space

pool.rationale:
DUSN is caused by nematodes: Ancylostoma caninum, T canis, Baylisascaris procyonis. The clinical course is characterized by unilateral vision loss from recurrent episodes of focal, multifocal, and diffuse inflammation of the retina, retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), and optic nerve.
The differential diagnosis includes sarcoidosis-associated uveitis, multifocal choroiditis, acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE), multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS), serpiginous choroidopathy, Behçet disease, ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (OHS), and ocular toxoplasmosis. Later stages show retinal arteriolar narrowing, optic atrophy, diffuse pigment epithelial degeneration, and abnormal electroretinography.
The diagnosis is most strongly supported by the observation of the worm in the subretinal space.
Results of systemic laboratory evaluations are typically negative for patients with DUSN.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In contrast to other white dot syndromes, what feature is invariably absent in punctate inner choroiditis (PIC)?
pool.rationale: Punctate inner choroiditis/choroidopathy (PIC) is classically a disease of young myopic females that is most commonly bilateral, although the findings may be asymmetric. It is characterized by small white-yellow chorioretinal lesions (100-200 μm) that rarely extend to the midperiphery. In contrast to other white dot syndromes, which typically have variable degrees of vitritis, these lesions are never associated with vitritis. These lesions can be accompanied by decreased visual acuity as well as central or paracentral scotomas. Choroidal neovascularization is a common complication that can threaten visual outcomes.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What ocular inflammatory condition is most likely to require alkylating agent therapy to achieve inflammation control?
pool.rationale:
Birdshot retinochoroidopathy is characterized by multifocal, hypopigmented, cream-colored, ovoid lesions at the level of choroid and retina pigment epithelium (RPE). Retinal vasculitis, cystoid macular edema (CME), and optic nerve involvement are other associations of the disease. Vision-threatening complications are CME, choroidal neovascular membrane, epiretinal membrane, optic atrophy. To prevent these complications, treatment with corticosteroids, or corticosteroid-sparing antimetabolites are indicated. Birdshot retinochoroidopathy is usually responsive to these measures, and alkylating agents are not indicated in most cases.
After infectious agents are ruled out, patients with intermediate uveitis are treated with local or systemic corticosteroids. In cases with poor response antimetabolites, calcineurin inhibitors can be tried. Very rarely, cyclophosphamide may be needed.
Alkylating agents such as cyclophosphamide and chlorambucil are usually used if other immunomodulatory agents fail. They are used as a first line of therapy for mucous membrane pemphigoid with active conjunctival inflammation and symblepharon, necrotizing scleritis secondary to systemic vasculitides, sympathetic ophthalmia, Behçet disease, and Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome.
Ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (OHS) presents with multiple, atrophic chorioretinal scars (histo-spots); peripapillary pigment changes, and choroidal neovascular membranes without vitreous cells. The acute, granulomatous lesions of OHS can be treated with oral or local corticosteroids. Alkylating agents are usually not indicated. The main causes of vision loss in such patients are juxtafoveal, subfoveal, or peripapillary choroidal neovascular (CNV) membranes. These are treated with thermal laser photocoagulation, photodynamic therapy (PDT), submacular surgery to remove CNV membranes, and intravitreal injection of anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) agents.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What congenital infection is most likely to manifest with intracranial calcifications, chorioretinal scars, nystagmus, and optic atrophy?
pool.rationale:
Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) is a single-stranded RNA virus of the Arenaviridae family; rodents are the natural hosts and reservoir. Transmission is thought to be airborne, from contamination of food by infected rodent excreta, or possibly from the bite of an infected animal. Symptomatic maternal illness occurs in approximately two-thirds of cases, with vertical transmission to the fetus occurring during episodes of maternal viremia. Systemic findings include macrocephaly, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications. Neurologic abnormalities, seizures, and mild cognitive impairment may be present. Ocular findings include macular and chorioretinal peripheral scarring, similar in morphology and distribution to that of congenital toxoplasmosis. Other findings include optic atrophy, strabismus, and nystagmus.
Congenital rubella demonstrates cardiac malformations, chorioretinitis, cataracts, corneal clouding, microphthalmia, strabismus, glaucoma, and deafness. Cysticercosis may present with a leukocoric eye. When the brain is involved with cysticercosis, intracerebral calcifications or hydrocephalus can be found. Cysticercosis is typically acquired from ingestion of contaminated water or food. Congenital West Nile virus is rare and, to date, one case has been reported with chorioretinal scars, but no intracranial calcifications.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In what setting is the use of tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha inhibitors contraindicated?

options.b: posterior uveitis in a child younger than 10 years old
options.d: intermediate uveitis associated with periventricular T2 changes on cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)

pool.rationale: TNF-alpha inhibitors are approved for the treatment of noninfectious uveitis. The use of TNF-alpha inhibitors is associated with worsening on demyelinating lesions in the brain and should not be used in patients with intermediate uveitis when the disease is associated with multiple sclerosis or demyelinating lesions.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What receptor is strongly involved in lipopolysaccharide-induced uveitis?

options.d: cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 on T cells

pool.rationale:
Lipopolysaccharide-induced uveitis involves innate immunity or natural immunity. Innate immunity does not require prior contact with the inciting stimulus. The 2 major effector cells of innate immunity are neutrophils and macrophages. The most important triggering molecules of innate immunity are lipopolysaccharides. The primary receptors of lipopolysaccharides are toll-like receptors (TLR), especially TLR2 and TLR4, which are expressed on macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells, and lymphocytes.
Adaptive immune response is a complex arc of response to highly variable but specific antigenic epitopes that are NOT self. It involves antigen-presenting cells, T cells, and B cells. Within the adaptive immune response, cytotoxic T cells stimulate apoptosis of target cells using the CD95 ligand (FasL).
Interleukin 17 is a pro-inflammatory cytokine produced by T-helper cells. IL-17 binds to a type I cell surface receptor called IL-17R, of which there are at least 3 variants: IL17RA, IL17RB, and IL17RC.
Cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 is a protein receptor that downregulates the immune system. CTLA4 is found on the surface of T cells, and acts as an "off" switch when bound to CD80 or CD86 on the surface of antigen-presenting cells.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient with acute unilateral anterior uveitis presents with an intraocular pressure of 35 mm Hg three days into treatment with frequent topical steroids. Examination with a slit lamp demonstrates a deep anterior chamber, 3+ cell and 2 clock hours of posterior synechiae. What is the most likely cause of increased intraocular pressure?
pool.rationale: Elevated intraocular pressure in eyes with uveitis can result from several factors. In acute uveitis, intraocular pressure may be increased due to decreased aqueous outflow through inflamed trabecular meshwork, or through meshwork obstructed with inflammatory debris. Pupillary block glaucoma can result from circumferential posterior synechiae and seclusion of the pupil. Inflammation of the ciliary body can result in aqueous hyposecretion and result in hypotony or labile intraocular pressure when both the ciliary body and the trabecular meshwork are inflamed. Steroid-response glaucoma rarely occurs prior to 3 weeks of treatment, and clinicians should resist the urge to prematurely taper corticosteroids because of corticosteroid-induced ocular hypertension.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with unilateral blurred vision and is found to have large keratic precipitates, extensive posterior synechiae, iris nodules, 2+ anterior chamber cells, vitreous cells, and peripheral vascular sheathing. What study result would help support the ophthalmologist's suspected diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Per the International Workshop on Ocular Sarcoidosis (IWOS), presence of bilateral hilar adenopathy with a compatible uveitis (and without a biopsy) is consistent with "presumed ocular sarcoidosis." The ultimate means of diagnosis in sarcoidosis is biopsy, which typically reveals noncaseating granulomas.
Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome has a strong association with HLA-DR4 among Japanese patients and with HLA-DR1 or HLA-DR4 among Hispanic patients from southern California. Positive pathergy testing is seen in Behçet disease. Dalen-Fuchs nodules are yellowish white mid-equatorial choroidal lesions in sympathetic ophthalmia. VKH syndrome, Behçet disease, and sympathetic ophthalmia, along with sarcoidosis, are all causes of panuveitis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What therapeutic agent, used in the treatment of severe uveitis, permanently cross-links deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and has the highest risk of secondary malignancy?
pool.rationale:
Patients with uveitis/scleritis that is non-responsive to corticosteroids or that requires doses of corticosteroids too high for long-term use should be transitioned to steroid-sparing immunomodulatory therapy (IMT). Antimetabolites such as methotrexate, azathioprine, and mycophenolate mofetil have been used successfully. Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating agent that permanently cross-links DNA. Although it is very effective in controlling inflammation, there is a significant risk of myelosuppression, secondary infections, and subsequent neoplasia. Of these agents, cyclophosphamide has the highest risk of secondary malignancy. Hemorrhagic cystitis is also a known complication of cyclophosphamide use and can be minimized by increasing water consumption.
Azathioprine, a purine nucleoside analogue, interferes with DNA replication and RNA transcription. Gastrointestinal upset is a common side effect of azathioprine. Serious side effects that are less common include hepatotoxicity and bone marrow suppression. Mycophenolate mofetil inhibits both inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase and DNA replication. Reversible gastrointestinal distress and diarrhea are common side effects. Methotrexate is a folic acid analogue and inhibitor of dihydrofolate reductase; it inhibits DNA replication, but its anti-inflammatory effects result from extracellular release of adenosine. Folate is given concurrently to reduce the risk of side effects. Gastrointestinal distress and anorexia may occur in 10% of patients. Reversible hepatotoxicity occurs in up to 15% of patients, and cirrhosis occurs in less than 0.1 % of patients receiving long-term methotrexate. Methotrexate is teratogenic, and complete blood cell counts and liver function tests should be obtained every 4 to 6 weeks to monitor for side effects.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 37-year-old woman with AIDS and a CD4+ count of 5 cells/μL develops loss of vision in her left eye. Her funduscopic examination is shown in the photograph. What slit-lamp feature would be expected?
pool.rationale: Patients with AIDS are at risk for several opportunistic infections. At CD4+ cell counts < 50/μL, these patients can incur cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis, which is what this patient has. The anterior uveitis and vitritis in CMV retinitis is mild; there is no ciliary flush or hypopyon, and no large keratic precipitates are present. However,  patients with a history of CMV retinitis can develop a severe uveitis if they are treated with potent combination antiretroviral therapy but without concomitant administration of ganciclovir, even though their CMV retinitis may currently be inactive.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient with retinal vasculitis also has necrotizing pulmonary granulomas and nephritis. What serum antibody is most likely to be associated with this entity?
pool.rationale: The case described appears to be a retinal vasculitis associated with a systemic granulomatous process affecting both lungs and kidneys. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is the most likely condition that would fit this description; therefore, the correct serum antibody is ANCA. Approximately 10% of patients with GPA can manifest retinal vascular involvement. Systemic lupus erythematosus (as suggested by ANA) does not result in pulmonary granulomas, although it can produce a retinal vasculitis and nephritis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient with AIDS and cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis in 1 eye undergoes successful placement of an intravitreal ganciclovir implant without systemic anti-CMV therapy and also receives highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Ten months later, the retinitis is inactive, and the patient's CD4+ count is 200 cells/µL. What would be the most appropriate approach for treatment of the retinitis at this time?

options.b: Remove the ganciclovir implant and place another one at the same surgical site.
options.c: Leave the implant in place and insert another one in a different quadrant.

pool.rationale:
Treatment of CMV retinitis involves 3 steps: immune reconstitution with HAART and concomitant treatment of the virus (intravenous ganciclovir or foscarnet, oral valganciclovir, or intravitreal ganciclovir or foscarnet [see Table 11-3]); maintenance of antiviral therapy for 3-6 months to allow for adequate immune reconstitution (despite early recovery of CD4+ cell counts); continued HAART therapy without antivirals, with dilated fundus examinations every 3 months (because immune reconstitution uveitis [IRU] can occur in patients on HAART with a history of prior CMV retinitis, even if the retinitis is currently inactive and CD4+ counts are >50 cells/µL; IRU tends to occur more frequently in eyes with more than 25% of the retinal surface involved in prior CMV infections).
In the case described, at 10 months out from initial infection, on HAART, and with CD4+ counts of 200 cells/µL, this patient is immune reconstituted from a CMV risk standpoint and can safely be observed off antiviral treatment with dilated fundus examinations every 3 months. (Note that the ganciclovir implant lasts for approximately 8 months, which is ample time to allow for immune reconstitution on HAART, as oral valganciclovir therapy in this setting is typically discontinued 6 months after the initiation of HAART). There is no need to replace or remove the ganciclovir implant in the absence of new signs of CMV infection, which is unlikely at CD4+ counts >50 cells/µL (although, as stated earlier, IRU can still occur while patients are on HAART, and as such these patients should be monitored every 3 months).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What antiparasitic therapy is most commonly used to slow the progression of onchocerciasis?
pool.rationale: Ivermectin, given every 3 to 6 months, as long as there is evidence of skin or eye infection (along with a 6-week course of doxycycline), is the treatment of choice for onchocerciasis. Ivermectin safely kills the microfilariae, but it does not have a permanent effect on the adult worms. Doxycycline targets Wolbachia, a parasitic bacterium that infects the adult worms and is crucial to their sexual development. Elimination of Wolbachia generally sterilizes and hastens the death of the worms.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What kind of scleritis is most likely to be associated with systemic disease that has high mortality?
pool.rationale: Necrotizing scleritis is the most severe and destructive type of scleritis, and more likely to lead to vision loss. It is more frequently associated with systemic disease (approximately 50%-60% of cases), some being life-threatening systemic vasculitic diseases. Necrotizing scleritis more frequently affects older individuals, and is more prevalent in women. Patients with necrotizing scleritis and who were not diagnosed timely suffered from mortality rates as high as 30%.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the first-line treatment in patients with unilateral nodular anterior scleritis and no known systemic disease association?
pool.rationale: Oral NSAIDs are first-line therapy for nodular anterior scleritis, as long as infectious causes have been excluded and there are no contraindications to NSAID use. Topical corticosteroids will have minimal to no effect in this setting, while oral corticosteroids and IMT are reserved for more severe cases and those refractory to oral NSAIDs.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What white dot syndrome can be mimicked by tuberculosis infection?

options.b: acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy

pool.rationale:
It is important to distinguish presumed immune-mediated serpiginous choroiditis from infectious entities that can simulate the disease. Although herpetic and syphilitic choroiditis can occasionally mimic serpiginous choroiditis, much more commonly, Mycobacterium tuberculosis can cause inflammation in a similar pattern. Results of tuberculin skin testing and the interferon-gamma release assay are usually positive for tuberculosis, although the chest x-ray often appears normal. The disease usually responds to anti-tuberculosis treatment, and corticosteroids may also be needed to control inflammation.
An infectious etiology has not been suggested for acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (although it may be preceded by viral prodrome), birdshot chorioretinopathy, or punctate inner choroiditis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What virus or virus family is most often implicated in glaucomatocyclitic crisis (Posner-Schlossman syndrome [PSS])?
pool.rationale:
The herpesvirus family of viruses (namely cytomegalovirus [CMV]) has been most often implicated in PSS, indicating a possible role for antiviral therapy.
The most common ocular manifestation of congenital rubella syndrome is unilateral or bilateral pigmentary retinopathy.
Multifocal chorioretinitis is characteristic of West Nile virus.
Hepatitis B virus has been implicated in polyarteritis nodosa.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Vitreous biopsy should be considered in cases of uveitis if what condition is suspected?
pool.rationale:
Primary intraocular lymphoma (also known as primary vitreoretinal lymphoma and previously known as reticulum cell sarcoma) masquerades as chronic uveitis in patients above the age of 50 (peak 75-84 years old). Lymphoma will frequently respond to topical or systemic corticosteroids, but it is often not until it recurs or becomes recalcitrant to steroid therapy that a neoplastic cause is entertained. The gold standard for diagnosing intraocular lymphoma is histologic confirmation of atypical lymphocytes, which requires vitrectomy. Further studies that can be performed on the vitrectomy specimen for lymphoma include high IL-10 to IL-6 ratio (supportive only, not diagnostic), immunohistochemistry for lambda or kappa light chains, flow cytometry (evaluating for a clonal population of B-cells or T-cells), and IgH gene or T-cell receptor (TCR) gene rearrangement to elucidate monoclonality that typify a neoplastic, lymphomatous process. A vitrectomy can be not only diagnostic, but also therapeutic in cases of lymphoma, as it can remove visually significant vitritis. Vitreous biopsy can be negative in one-third of cases, so repeat vitrectomy/vitreous biopsy should be considered if high suspicion exists and the initial biopsy is negative.
Vitrectomy should not be considered for retinoblastoma, as intraocular surgery could lead to seeding of neoplastic cells into the orbit. Traumatic uveitis is typically ascertained with an appropriate history of trauma and will respond to topical corticosteroids. Uveitis related to HLA-B27 positive disease (including psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis) is typically a recurrent uveitis. Diagnostic vitrectomy is not indicated for this condition.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the definitive treatment for a patient with phacoantigenic uveitis?

options.c: oral methotrexate following baseline hepatic function tests
options.d: topical prednisolone acetate drops given hourly

pool.rationale: An immune reaction to lens material may result in ocular inflammatory disease. This reaction may follow disruption of the lens capsule (traumatic or surgical), termed phacoantigenic uveitis, or leakage of lens protein through the intact lens capsule in mature or hypermature cataracts, termed phacolytic uveitis. While antiinflammatory medications may be used to reduce inflammation, the definitive treatment is to remove the inciting lens material.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the first step in the delayed hypersensitivity reaction that occurs in a positive purified protein derivative (PPD) test?

options.a: T lymphocytes primed in the hilar nodes circulating to the dermis
options.c: cytokines within the dermis inducing filtration of lymphocytes, monocytes and fibrin clotting
options.d: dermal macrophages ingesting the purified protein derivative (PPD) reagent

pool.rationale:
Following exposure to live tuberculin organisms in the lungs, alveolar macrophages ingest the microorganisms and travel to the hilar lymph nodes. B and T lymphocytes are primed and then recirculate to the lungs. Once the T lymphocytes encounter macrophage-ingested TB, cytokines are released that induce neighboring macrophages to differentiate into epithelioid cells and become caseating granulomas. A secondary skin response to injection of purified protein derivative (PPD) begins with dermal macrophages ingesting the antigen. These PPD-stimulated macrophages migrate into an adjacent lymph node, where they encounter memory T lymphocytes. The memory T lymphocytes then recirculate into the dermis, where they encounter other stimulated macrophages at the injection site. This fully activates the memory  T lymphocytes to release cytokines locally. These cytokines induce infiltration of additional T lymphocytes, monocytes, and fibrin clotting forming the indurated dermal lesion. Because this occurs in approximated 24 hours, it is called a delayed hypersensitivity reaction.
Type I hypersensitivity is triggered by the activation of IgE. The Fc portion of the IgE antibody binds to mast cells, causing them to degranulate and release interleukins and cytokines. This happens within several minutes of re-exposure. These inflammatory mediators can cause blood vessel dilation and massive edema, leading to reactions ranging from hives and urticaria to laryngeal edema and anaphylaxis. Type II hypersensitivity is defined as a hypersensitivity reaction secondary to antibodies that are directly cytotoxic against human tissues. Examples of Type II hypersensitivity include Goodpasture syndrome and cicatricial pemphigoid. Type III hypersensitivity is defined as a hypersensitivity secondary to antibody-antigen immune complex reactions. Examples of Type III hypersensitivity include systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 70-year-old woman had cataract surgery. If a chronic, indolent, intraocular inflammation develops, what organism aside from Propionibacterium acnes should be suspected?
pool.rationale:
Candida parapsilosis

Although all the organisms listed can cause endophthalmitis, only Candida parapsilosis causes an indolent chronic inflammation similar to that which occurs with Propionibacterium acnes.

pool.q: What is the immunologic mechanism for type IV hypersensitivity?

options.a: Recognition of antigen by memory T cells results in activation and amplification of clones that react to the specific antigen still present in the skin.
options.b: Antibody-mediated cytotoxicity triggers apoptosis of epidermal keratocytes.
options.c: Deposition of antigen-antibody immune complexes results in activation of complement and attracts tissue macrophages.
options.d: Activation of IgE receptors on eosinophils results in release of histamine, leukotrienes, and other inflammatory mediators.

pool.rationale: A prototypical type 4 delayed hypersensitivity reaction is poison ivy–related contact dermatitis. Upon first exposure to urushiol oil, the agent that causes this dermatitis, the antigen is taken to regional lymph nodes by antigen-presenting cells. Once lymphocytes are found that recognize this antigen, they enter the circulation, but only after the antigen is no longer found in the skin. Subsequent exposures, however, result in activation of memory lymphocytes that produce clinical signs of inflammation within 24 to 36 hours. IgE mediates allergic-type immune reactions, and antigen antibody immune complexes mediate serum sickness and may be part of the immunopathogenesis of vasculitis. Antibody-mediated cytotoxicity is a mechanism of removing infected or neoplastic cells.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What percentage of patients with ankylosing spondylitis have a positive HLA B27 ?
pool.rationale:
Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) ranges in severity from asymptomatic to crippling. Symptoms of this disorder include lower back pain and morning stiffness. Up to 90% of patients with AS test positive for HLA-B27, although most HLA-B27–positive individuals do not develop the disease. The chance that an HLA-B27–positive patient will develop spondyloarthritis or eye disease is 1 in 4. Family members may also have AS or anterior uveitis. Often, persons with anterior uveitis lack symptoms of back disease.
Approximately 40%–50% of patients with acute anterior uveitis are HLA-B27 positive. Thus, although patients with recurrent anterior nongranulomatous uveitis should be tested for HLA-B27, the presence of HLA-B27 alone does not provide an absolute diagnosis. Several autoimmune diseases known collectively as the seronegative spondyloarthropathies are strongly associated with both acute anterior uveitis and HLA-B27 including reactive arthritis syndrome, inflammatory bowel disease, psoriatic arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis. Women are more likely than men to experience the atypical spondyloarthropathies.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 62-year-old, nondiabetic patient underwent cataract surgery with intraocular lens (IOL) placement 6 months ago. Initially, vision improved to 20/25, but 2 months later the patient had several episodes of recurrent inflammation, requiring treatment with topical steroids. The patient now presents with a small hypopyon. What is the appropriate treatment for this patient?

options.a: pars plana vitrectomy and intraocular lens removal
options.d: pars plana vitrectomy (PPV), partial capsulectomy, and injection of intravitreal and endocapsular antibiotics

pool.rationale:
The patient's presentation is consistent with chronic postoperative endophthalmitis, most commonly caused by Propionibacterium acnes.
The preferred treatment includes pars plana vitrectomy, partial capsulectomy, and injection of intravitreal and endocapsular vancomycin. pool.q: What would anterior chamber paracentesis of a patient with phacolytic uveitis most likely reveal?

The cytoplasmic, or c-ANCA, pattern is both sensitive and specific for GPA and is present in up to 95% of patients; proteinase 3 is the most common target antigen (referred to as PR3-ANCA).

pool.q: A patient is being treated for first-time presentation of undifferentiated granulomatous iridocyclitis. options.d: Schedule the patient for glaucoma valve placement.

pool.q: A 65-year-old man is found to have unilateral decline in vision as well as occlusive arteritis, vitritis, and a multifocal yellow-white peripheral retinitis. What is the best therapy?

Patients with acute retinal necrosis usually present with acute unilateral loss of vision, photophobia, floaters, and pain. Panuveitis is observed, beginning with significant anterior segment inflammation with keratic precipitates, posterior synechiae, and elevated intraocular pressure, together with heavy vitreous cellular infiltration. Within 2 weeks, the classic triad of occlusive retinal arteriolitis, vitritis, and a multifocal yellow-white peripheral retinitis has evolved. Widespread necrosis of the midperipheral retina, multiple posterior retinal breaks, and proliferative vitreoretinopathy predispose to combined tractional–rhegmatogenous retinal detachments in 75% of patients. Timely diagnosis and prompt antiviral therapy are essential given the rapidity of disease progression, the frequency of retinal detachment, and the guarded visual prognosis.
Intravenous acyclovir, 10 mg/kg every 8 hours for 10–14 days, is effective against herpes simplex virus and varicella-zoster virus. After 24–48 hours of antiviral therapy, systemic corticosteroids (prednisone, 1 mg/kg/day) are introduced to treat active inflammation and subsequently tapered over several weeks. Aspirin and other anticoagulants have been used to treat an associated hypercoagulable state and prevent vascular occlusions, but the results have been inconclusive. More recently, oral valacyclovir at doses of up to 2 g, 3 times daily, has been used successfully as an alternative to intravenous acyclovir as induction therapy. Additionally, intravitreal ganciclovir (0.2–2.0 mg/0.1 mL) and foscarnet (1.2–2.4 mg/0.1 mL) have been used to achieve a rapid induction in combination with both intravenous and oral antivirals as first-line therapy or in patients who fail to respond to systemic acyclovir.

pool.q: A 29-year-old woman presents for evaluation of bilateral central vision loss and photopsias. She reports onset of fever, chills, headache, and malaise approximately 1 week ago. Symptoms are typically bilateral, with fellow eye involvement occurring within a period of days to weeks. Typical fundus findings include large (1-2 disc diameters), yellow-white, placoid lesions distributed throughout the posterior pole to the equator. Fundus angiography typically demonstrates early hypofluorescence corresponding to the lesions but often exceeding the areas visible funduscopically. In late phases, these lesions demonstrate late hypofluorescent staining. These lesions typically involute over a period of several weeks, leaving behind significant retinal pigment epithelial alteration.
Most patients recover visual function of 20/40 or better, although there are often residual visual deficits. APMPPE is associated with HLA-B7 and HLA-DR2 and is thought to be an immune-driven vasculitis. The most serious complication associated with APMPPE is the development of cerebral vasculitis.

pool.q: A 52-year-old man presents with bilateral panuveitis and retinal vasculitis. He also has complaints of arthralgia, diplopia, diarrhea, and poor performance at work. What test may help with the diagnosis?
pool.rationale: Whipple disease is a rare multisystem disease caused by the Tropheryma whipplei bacterium. It is most common in middle-aged white men. Migratory arthritis occurs in 80% of cases, and diarrhea, steatorrhea, and malabsorption occur in 75%. Central nervous system involvement occurs in 10% of cases and results in seizures, dementia, and coma. Neuro-ophthalmic signs can include cranial nerve palsies, nystagmus, and ophthalmoplegia. Intraocular involvement occurs in less than 5% of cases. Patients can present with bilateral panuveitis, retinal vasculitis, and multifocal chorioretinitis. The gold standard for diagnosis of Whipple disease is a duodenal biopsy that demonstrates a periodic acid–Schiff–positive bacillus in macrophages within intestinal villi.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Band keratopathy is a common complication in what form of uveitis?
pool.rationale: Band keratopathy is a complication of chronic intraocular inflammation, typically more common when the predominant site of inflammation is the anterior segment. Of the choices provided, only JIA-associated anterior uveitis is a chronic uveitis. HLA-B27-associated uveitis and herpetic iridocyclitis are both acute, episodic forms of uveitis and typically do not result in band keratopathy (Note: inadequately treated forms of B27 acute anterior uveitis can take on a more "chronic" nature that can eventually produce band keratopathy, but this is not common). Toxoplasma-associated uveitis is predominantly a posterior uveitis that is also episodic in nature and does not typically result in band keratopathy. Aggressive inflammation associated with toxoplasmosis can produce anterior segment inflammation, as well, but the episodic nature of this type of inflammation precludes the chronic inflammation necessary to produce band keratopathy.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What immunosuppressive drug used to treat noninfectious ocular inflammation is most clearly associated with an increased risk of malignancy?
pool.rationale:
Alkylating agents include cyclophosphamide and chlorambucil. The most worrisome adverse effect of these agents is an increased risk of malignancy. There drugs should be used with great caution.
Azathioprine and methotrexate are antimetabolites, and cyclosporine is a T-cell inhibitor. The Systemic Immunosuppressive Therapy for Eye Diseases (SITE) cohort study of 7957 patients with noninfectious uveitis showed that patients who took azathioprine, methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporine, or systemic corticosteroids had overall cancer mortality rates similar to those who never took those medications. There was a non-statistically significant increase in cancer-related mortality rates in patients treated with cyclophosphamide.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In what stage of syphilis infection can a syphilitic gumma be seen?
pool.rationale: Gummatous syphilis is very uncommon in the present era. Gummas are heaped up granulomatous lesions with a round, irregular, or serpiginous shape. They can occur anywhere, including skin, bones, or internal organs. Gummatous syphilis remains the most uncommon type of tertiary syphilis. Other subcategories of tertiary syphilis include cardiovascular syphilis and neurosyphilis, with ocular syphilis being considered a variant of the latter.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What tissue is more effectively evaluated with indocyanine green angiography than with fluorescein angiography?
pool.rationale:
Indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) is used to evaluate the choroid, including choroidal perfusion and lesions within the choroid.
Imaging of the inner retina is best performed with optical coherence tomography. The pars plana is best imaged with wide-field fundus photography and fluorescein angiography. The ciliary body can be evaluated at least in part with gonioscopy, but anterior segment ultrasound biomicroscopy is excellent at imaging this structure.

pool.q: A 68-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) with severe lung disease. He reports sudden pain and vision loss in the right eye and is noted to have a macular infiltrate with a subretinal hypopyon and involvement of retinal and choroidal vessels. Minimal vitritis is present and the anterior segment is relatively quiet. What fungal pathogen is most likely causative?
pool.rationale:
Aspergillus

Endogenous Aspergillus endophthalmitis is typically seen in patients with severe chronic pulmonary disease, immunocompromise, endocarditis, or intravenous (IV) drug abuse. Disseminated infection most commonly involves the lung, with the eye as the second most common site of infection.
Unlike Candida endophthalmitis, in which the vitreous is the main focus of infection, the main foci of Aspergillus infections are the subretinal space and retinal and choroidal vessels. Because Aspergillus often involves the macula, visual outcomes are poor.
Ocular coccidioidomycosis is rare and typically manifests with blepharitis, phlyctenular and granulomatous conjunctivitis, or more uncommonly, with granulomatous anterior uveitis, iris granulomas, or multifocal chorioretinitis.
Ocular cryptococcus is often seen in patients with HIV and is frequently associated with meningitis. Papilledema, cranial nerve palsies, and multifocal chorioretinitis are seen.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What intervention is most likely to limit the inflammatory sequelae of ocular cysticercosis?
pool.rationale: Death of the larvae results in significant intraocular inflammation. As such, removal of the intraocular cyst via vitrectomy, without killing the contained larvae, results in the least amount of intraocular inflammation.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common form of intraocular involvement in patients with sarcoid panuveitis?
pool.rationale:
Although all of these features can be seen in ocular sarcoidosis, chronic anterior uveitis is the most frequently encountered form (up to 80% in some series).
Posterior segment manifestations occur in up to 20% of patients with ocular sarcoidosis. Vitreous involvement is common and often presents as clumps of snowballs with or without diffuse cellular infiltration. Occlusive retinal vascular disease, especially branch retinal vein occlusion and, less commonly, central retinal vein occlusion, together with peripheral retinal capillary nonperfusion, may lead to retinal neovascularization and vitreous hemorrhage. Sarcoid may also be associated with an inflammatory optic neuropathy, with or without concurrent intraocular inflammation.
