pool.q: What finding in vitreous samples can help to support the diagnosis of intraocular lymphoma?

options.b: high ratio of IL-10 to IL-6
options.c: high ratio of IL-6 to IL-10

pool.rationale:
Cytokine analysis of vitreous samples can be helpful in supporting the diagnosis of intraocular lymphoma. Interleukin-10 (IL-10) levels are elevated in the vitreous of patients with lymphoma. In contrast, high levels of IL-6 are found in the vitreous of patients with inflammatory uveitis. Thus, the ratio of IL-10 to IL-6 is often elevated in intraocular lymphoma and supports the diagnosis. Gene rearrangement studies can provide evidence of monoclonality. Flow cytometry may reveal kappa (κ) or gamma (γ) chain restriction or large B-cell populations, both of which support the diagnosis of B-cell lymphoma. A specific mutation (proline for leucine substitution mutation at position 265) of the myeloid differentiation primary response 88 protein (MYD88) is also supportive.
If diagnosis by vitreous aspiration or subretinal aspiration cannot be established, internal or external chorioretinal biopsy techniques may be useful in the diagnosis of PCNSL.
Cytologic specimens obtained from the vitreous or subretinal space often show pleomorphic cells with scanty cytoplasm, hyperchromatic nuclei with multiple irregular nucleoli, and an elevated nuclear-to-cytoplasm ratio. Monoclonality of cells is likely to be present in PCNSL. This can be established through immunophenotyping by immunohistochemistry or flow cytometry to demonstrate the clonality of B lymphocytes by the presence of abnormal immunoglobulin κ or γ light chain predominance, specific B-lymphocyte markers (CD19, CD20, and CD22), and/or gene or oncogene translocations or gene rearrangements. Abnormal lymphocytes may be isolated manually or by laser capture and polymerase chain reaction (PCR)–based assays performed to improve the diagnostic yield of paucicellular samples. See also BCSC Section 4, Ophthalmic Pathology and Intraocular Tumors, for discussion of intraocular lymphoma.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is an expected side effect associated with a tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) inhibitor?
pool.rationale: Because TNF-α inhibitors interfere with the TNF signaling pathway involved in mediating inflammation (which can be an important response in fighting infection), the use of such medications can increase the patient's susceptibility to infection. Thus, tuberculosis is typically evaluated prior to starting an anti-TNF medication. Additionally, it is important to determine whether patients at risk for certain fungal infections live in an area where those infections are endemic.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What ocular finding would be expected in a patient infected with chikungunya virus?
pool.rationale: The ocular features of chikungunya virus infection include anterior uveitis and retinitis. The anterior uveitis may be characterized by pigmented keratic precipitates, iris pigment release, and, like other types of viral anterior uveitides, elevated intraocular pressure. Varying amounts of vitritis can be seen, and the posterior segment findings involve a retinitis characterized by focal, multifocal, or confluent retinitis, occasionally with retinal hemorrhages.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 72-year-old man reports several episodes of vision loss in his right eye over the past few months. He has no ocular history other than uncomplicated cataract surgery in both eyes 3 years ago. The patient has covered either eye and confirms that the vision loss is isolated to his right eye. He describes the vision loss as a "white out" that comes on over several minutes, leaves him severely visually disabled for several hours, and then gradually clears back to his normal baseline vision over 1 to 2 hours. He has had eye examinations following each of these episodes in the past. They showed mild phacodonesis in the right eye but were otherwise unremarkable. Prior workup to rule out giant cell arteritis was negative. The patient is frustrated that despite multiple examinations, an etiology has not been found. What would be the most helpful thing to do on his visit today to help yield a diagnosis?

options.a: refer to cardiology for a Holter monitor

pool.rationale:
Whenever a patient complains of vision loss in 1 eye only, it is imperative to know whether the visual loss involves the right eye or the right field of vision. Unless a patient has covered each eye alternately, they cannot know this. In this question, the patient was reliable and had confirmed the vision loss was only in 1 eye. The second issue is the nature of the vision loss. Amaurosis fugax is characterized by temporary loss of all sight in the eye (a "blackout"). However, this patient describes a "white out," which is more characteristic of a transient obscuring of the ocular media, especially considering the long duration of the vision loss and the slow recovery over 1-2 hours.
In any patient with symptoms suggestive of transient obscuring of the ocular media, who is also pseudophakic, uveitis-glaucoma-hyphema (UGH) syndrome should be considered. In UGH syndrome, chafing of the iris by the optic/bag complex or the haptics causes transient intraocular bleeds. Gonioscopy is the key to the diagnosis of UGH, especially after the vision has cleared. A small layer of hemorrhage in the inferior angle provides evidence of the transient bleed. Although originally described as a complication of iris chafing by closed-loop anterior chamber intraocular lenses (IOLs), UGH syndrome is now more commonly seen with PCIOLs.
Automated visual field testing would be beneficial if a homonymous defect were suspected, as opposed to loss of vision restricted to 1 eye. Likewise, referral to cardiology for a Holter monitor would be beneficial if symptoms consistent with vertebro-basilar insufficiency were suspected; however, loss of vision restricted to 1 eye makes this less likely.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the cause of hypotony in chronic anterior uveitis?

options.b: decreased aqueous production from the ciliary body
options.c: prolonged use (> 6 months) of oral corticosteroids
options.d: posterior synechiae resulting in iris bombé

pool.rationale:
Dysfunction of the ciliary body may be a sequela of chronic inflammation; this may be due to ciliary body detachment induced by cyclitic membranes, reversible dysfunction due to inflammation, or permanent dysfunction in the setting of ciliary body atrophy.
Anterior synechiae and posterior synechiae may lead to elevated intraocular pressure (IOP), but in some patients may be part of a delicate balance of decreased aqueous production and outflow; these patients may develop hypotony following intraocular surgery if aqueous outflow is improved.
Corticosteroids can increase IOP by reversing ciliary body dysfunction induced by inflammation or choroidal effusion, or by corticosteroid-induced glaucoma.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with a 1-week history of right eye pain and photophobia. On examination, there is mild injection of the bulbar conjunctiva, and 2+ cell and flare with no keratic precipitates. Her left eye is white and quiet. The ophthalmologist diagnoses nongranulomatous anterior uveitis. On review of systems, she notes that her knees have been very painful recently, and the ophthalmologist orders a number of tests. All test results are negative except for a positive anti-CCP (cyclic citrullinated protein antibodies) test result. What systemic disease is most likely?
pool.rationale:
This patient has a positive CCP test result. In addition to the rheumatoid factor (RF) test, the CCP test is helpful in diagnosing rheumatoid arthritis. The sensitivity and specificity is increased when both RF and CCP show positive results, but in the setting of painful joints, rheumatoid arthritis is the most likely diagnosis.
The spectrum of ocular findings in Lyme disease varies with stage of disease. Anterior, intermediate, or posterior uveitis, or panuveitis, may occur in Stage 2 Lyme disease. Intermediate uveitis is the most common presentation.
Tubulointerstitial nephritis occurs most commonly in adolescent girls, and a bilateral nongranulomatous anterior uveitis is the most common presentation. Workup reveals abnormal serum creatinine levels and abnormal urinalysis results, with elevated beta-2 microglobulin levels, proteinuria, and urinary white cell casts. Anterior uveitis is the most common ocular presentation of sarcoidosis.
The work up of sarcoidosis includes chest Xray or chest computed tomography (CT) scan, lysozyme level, and serum angiotensin converting enzyme level.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Following resolution of the white dots, what finding suggests the diagnosis of multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS)?

options.a: punched-out lesions in the retinal periphery
options.c: granular pigment changes in the fovea

pool.rationale: Subtle granular pigment changes in the fovea are present after the acute stage of MEWDS and they are considered pathognomonic for the disease. The finding can be very useful in diagnosing patients who present with symptoms after the white dots have faded. MEWDS patients do not typically develop peripheral punched-out lesions or peripapillary scarring, which can be present in ocular histoplasmosis syndrome and multifocal choroiditis. Perivascular pigment alterations can be present in retinal vasculitis, but not in MEWDS.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What disorder is most likely to cause a low-grade, unilateral, chronic, anterior uveitis and be associated with iris atrophy and transillumination defects?
pool.rationale:
Hallmark features of viral iridocyclitis include low-grade, chronic cells; diffuse, tiny keratic precipitates (KP) that do not remain within the Arlt triangle; iris atrophy; iris transillumination; and elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) during active flare-ups. A feature more specific to herpetic iridocyclitis is the presence of larger KP with overlying stromal edema secondary to the associated underlying endothelial dysfunction (ie, disciform keratitis). Although herpetic disease comes to mind in considering these examination findings, any viral iridocyclitis can present with these findings (except disciform keratitis, which is more specific to herpetic disease), although not as pronounced as when they occur with herpetic disease.
HLA-B27–associated acute anterior uveitis (AAU) can present with large keratic precipitates, a dense and fibrinous anterior chamber reaction with associated formation of posterior synechiae, and a hypopyon, but iris atrophy and transillumination are not typical of HLA-B27–associated disease.
VKH typically presents with bilateral exudative retinal detachments. Upon resolution of these detachments, future flare-ups do tend to present as low-grade anterior chamber reactions, but there is no associated iris atrophy or transillumination.
Sarcoidosis can present anywhere in the eye and can produce nongranulomatous and granulomatous inflammation (although the disease itself is granulomatous in nature); however, it does not result in iris atrophy or transillumination.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common ocular manifestation of syphilis?
pool.rationale: Syphilis is the "great imitator," but uveitis is the most common ocular manifestation or component of presentation. All of the other inflammatory features (localized choroiditis, cystoid macular edema, and neuroretinitis) may be present at a lesser frequency.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common cause of vision loss in pars planitis?
pool.rationale: Pars planitis refers to intermediate uveitis that is idiopathic. Cystoid macular edema is the number one cause of vision loss in pars planitis and can be chronic and refractory in up to 10% of patients. Other causes of vision loss in pars planitis include cataract, epiretinal membrane, and vitreous opacification. Vitreous hemorrhage can occur due to neovascularization in the peripheral retina but is not a common cause of vision loss. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachments can occur but are less common than serous or tractional detachments. Pars plana exudates, or snowbanks, can be seen in pars planitis and may indicate a more severe course, but they are not a major cause of vision loss.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What finding would be an indication for systemic immunomodulatory therapy in a child with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA)-associated iritis?

options.a: presence of posterior synechiae or band keratopathy
options.b: chronic anterior chamber cells on maximally tolerated local corticosteroid therapy
options.d: systemic immunomodulatory therapy is contraindicated in children with JIA-associated iritis.

pool.rationale:
The initial treatment of patients with JIA-associated uveitis includes topical corticosteroids. More severe cases require the use of systemic or periocular corticosteroids. However, long-term use of systemic corticosteroids can lead to complications such as growth retardation. Due to high ocular morbidity, these children should be treated with weekly, low-dose methotrexate. Methotrexate is effective, well tolerated and spares the complications associated with chronic ocular inflammation and systemic complications of corticosteroids. Recent studies also have shown the efficacy of tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitors in children with uveitis.
Presence of ANA is a risk factor for chronic iridocyclitis in patients with JIA, but is not an indication for systemic treatment in the absence of uveitis.
Posterior synechiae and band keratopathy are some of the ocular complications of JIA-associated uveitis, but not an indication for systemic treatment unless there is active uveitis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: For about how long does the fluocinolone acetonide implant release therapeutic levels of corticosteroids to the vitreous cavity?
pool.rationale: Multicenter, controlled clinical studies have shown that the 0.59-mg fluocinolone implant is effective for a median of 30 months. The sustained-release implant was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2005 for the treatment of chronic noninfectious uveitis affecting the posterior segment. The implant is inserted through a small pars plana incision and sutured to the sclera.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A woman with anterior and intermediate sarcoid uveitis exhibits less than ½+ anterior chamber cells, minimal vitreous haze, and no macular edema on mycophenolate and infliximab treatment. Before treatment, she exhibited 3+ anterior chamber cells, mutton-fat keratic precipitates, extensive posterior synechiae without iris bombé, and 2+ vitreous haze in both eyes. She now needs cataract surgery to drive. What is the best approach to cataract surgery?

options.a: Wait until her level of inflammation is stable on this regimen for at least 3 months and then perform cataract surgery.
options.c: Increase the infliximab dosage until there are absolutely no anterior chamber cells for 6 months.
options.d: Insert a fluocinolone implant and then perform cataract surgery as soon as possible.

pool.rationale: Ensuring that the current regimen is effective in controlling inflammation for at least 3 months and allowing the ocular tissues to recover from recent inflammation are both highly desirable. In some cases, it might not be necessary to wait 3 months; examples include a very mild uveitis that was easily controlled and is without sequelae as well as Fuchs heterochromic uveitis, which has a good surgical prognosis. The fluocinolone implant is unnecessary in this case because she is already being treated systemically, her disease is well controlled, and there is no macular edema. Reduction of anterior chamber cells to zero for 6 months is unnecessary.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the classic histologic description of phacoantigenic uveitis?
pool.rationale:
The typical histopathological appearance of phacoantigenic uveitis is a zonal granuloma centered around the site of the lens injury; neutrophils are present with surrounding lymphocytes, plasma cells, epithelioid cells, and occasional giant cells.
Macrophages with engorged lens proteins are thought to be the mechanism of trabecular meshwork obstruction in phacolytic glaucoma.
A purely polymorphonuclear leukocyte reaction is not typical, and an eosinophilic reaction is also not typical; for this reason, the old term phacoanaphylactic uveitis is not appropriate for this condition, because anaphylaxis involves immunoglobulin E (IgE), mast cells, and basophils, none of which are present in phacoantigenic uveitis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common noninfectious systemic disease associated with scleritis?
pool.rationale: About 40% of scleritis cases are associated with systemic disease, most commonly rheumatoid arthritis. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and systemic lupus erythematosus are also associated with scleritis, but much less frequently. Multiple sclerosis is associated with intermediate uveitis and pars planitis, not scleritis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What white blood cell can become an antigen-presenting cell?
pool.rationale: Basophils, eosinophils, and neutrophils do not have the ability to act as antigen-presenting cells. Only monocytes can be primed and induced to become antigen-presenting cells.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What osteoporosis therapy is most strongly implicated as a cause of ocular inflammatory disease?
pool.rationale: Bisphosphonates (such as alendronate, etidronate, risedronate, and zoledronic acid) have been associated with the development of uveitis. Other medications that have been associated with uveitis include oral contraceptives, rifabutin, sulfonamides, diethylcarbamazine, etanercept, topical metipranolol, topical prostaglandin analogues (PGAs), intravitreal cidofovir, and intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) injections.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 50-year-old man with a history of open-globe repair as a child presents with blurred vision and photophobia. Examination reveals bilateral panuveitis and subtle hypopigmented deep subretinal lesions. What is the most appropriate first step in treatment for the most likely cause of these findings?
pool.rationale:
Sympathetic ophthalmia should be suspected in any patient with a history of penetrating globe trauma who present complaining of blurred vision, photophobia, and ocular redness. Clinical findings, which are indistinguishable from those in Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome, include bilateral panuveitis, mutton fat keratic precipitates, exudative retinal detachments, and focal choroiditis. B-scan ultrasonography demonstrates choroidal thickening.
High-dose oral corticosteroids should be started immediately, but management with immunomodulatory agents is required in most patients. Topical corticosteroids are insufficient to address posterior disease. Intravitreal steroids are not standard of care for this bilateral disease.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What laboratory test would be most helpful in working up a patient whose condition is suspicious for multifocal choroiditis and panuveitis?

options.d: Herpes simplex virus (HSV1 and HSV2) polymerase chain reaction (PCR)

pool.rationale:
Multifocal choroiditis and panuveitis (MFC) is an idiopathic inflammatory disorder. It presents, mostly in young myopic women, with decreased vision, photopsias, and an enlarged blind spot. While HSV and EBV have been postulated, neither has been proven as causative, and MFC is still considered idiopathic and a diagnosis of exclusion. Because sarcoidosis, syphilis, and tuberculosis can produce lesions similar to those seen in MFC, those conditions should be ruled out through specific testing. Of the tests listed, RPR (and fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption [FTA-ABS]) would be most helpful to rule out syphilis, especially before starting steroid therapy.
EBV and HSV have been postulated but not proven to be causative of MFC. B. henselae is associated with cat-scratch disease and is classic for a macular star associated with optic nerve edema.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the primary cause of transient increases in intraocular pressure (IOP) in an eye with acute keratouveitis due to herpes simplex virus (HSV)?
pool.rationale:
Ocular hypertension associated with herpetic uveitis may be a helpful diagnostic hallmark. Most other inflammatory syndromes are associated with decreased intraocular pressure (IOP) that occurs as a result of ciliary body hyposecretion. However, herpesvirus may cause trabeculitis and thus increase IOP, often to as high as 50–60 mm Hg. In addition, inflammatory cells may contribute to trabecular obstruction and congestion.
Appositional angle closure, pupillary block, and increased episcleral venous pressure are not associated with acute HSV infection.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the preferred treatment for diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN)?
pool.rationale: Diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis is a posterior uveitis thought to be caused by a solitary nematode residing and migrating within the subretinal space. The dog hookworm Ancylostoma caninum and the larger raccoon roundworm Baylisascaris procyonis are believed to be the most common causative organisms. The disease features vitritis, optic nerve swelling, and multifocal inflammation of the retina and retinal pigment epithelium. Inflammatory lesions are typically multifocal, gray-white, and approximately 1 disc diameter in size. Occasionally, an s-shaped nematode is visible in the subretinal space. The preferred and most definitive treatment of DUSN is direct photocoagulation of the organism, which can halt further disease progression. Although systemic corticosteroids can treat inflammation, they do not treat the underlying cause. Systemic antihelminthics have had variable reported success. Vitrectomy is not indicated in the treatment of DUSN.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency department with dense anterior and posterior uveitis and seizures. He had been to India during the past few months. A cranial computed tomography (CT) scan shows a very small calcification and hydrocephalus. A B-scan shows a centrally echo-dense, curvilinear, highly reflective structure superior to the optic nerve. What is the cause of the patient's illness?
pool.rationale:
The B scan structure showing a centrally echo-dense, curvilinear, highly reflective structure superior to the optic nerve is suggestive of the scolex and is characteristic of cysticercosis.
Although the eye is more commonly affected than any other organ, neural cysticercosis is associated with significant morbidity and a mortality of 40%. Epileptiform seizures may be the first sign of cerebral cysticercosis. Both anterior chamber and vitreous may demonstrate inflammatory activity; vitreous inflammation is more pronounced during the early stages of the disease.
Anterior chamber paracentesis may reveal a large number of eosinophils; peripheral eosinophilia may also be present. Anticysticercus antibodies can be detected by ELISA in about 80% of patients with neural cysticercosis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What time course characterizes recurrent uveitis as defined by the Standardization of Uveitis Nomenclature (SUN) Working Group?

options.a: episodes of uveitis that recur more than 3 months after treatment has been discontinued
options.b: episodes of uveitis that recur irrespective of when treatment has been discontinued
options.c: episodes of uveitis that recur less than 3 months after treatment has been discontinued
options.d: episodes of uveitis that resolve in fewer than 3 months

pool.rationale: Episodes of uveitis that recur less than 3 months after treatment has been discontinued are classified as chronic uveitis. Acute uveitis is defined as resolving in fewer than 3 months. The answer choice “episodes of uveitis that recur irrespective of when treatment has been discontinued” is not a currently accepted classification of uveitis. Recurrent uveitis is classified as disease in which patients exhibit periods of quiescence that last longer than 3 months, off of therapy

pool.q: What is a contraindication to cataract surgery in a patient with uveitis?
pool.rationale:
The decision to perform cataract surgery in patients with uveitic eyes differs from considering this surgery for patients with nonuveitic eyes. The potential vision may be subnormal, due to previous macular edema or other permanent ocular damage. Active intraocular inflammation is a strong contraindication for surgery and should only be considered if the risks of delaying surgery outweigh the potential for dramatically exacerbating the inflammation. Complications can be minimized when inflammation has been controlled for several months before surgery and is treated aggressively after surgery.
Steroid-responsive glaucoma is not a contraindication for cataract surgery but should be considered when weighing the relative merits of periocular or intraocular corticosteroid use.
Many uveitis patients require systemic immunomodulatory therapy to obtain the necessary control of the inflammatory process before cataract surgery; the ideal scenario is absence of inflammatory cells, regardless of what specific therapies are required to achieve this state, before proceeding with cataract surgery.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Patients with what ocular inflammatory disorder might benefit from pars plana vitrectomy?
pool.rationale: Vitrectomy can be useful as a diagnostic tool if infectious or neoplastic vitreous infiltration is suspected, and it can also be useful in treating cases of inflammatory intermediate uveitis for visual rehabilitation. Removal of vitreous opacity, epiretinal membranes, repair of retinal detachments, and other primary indications can provide direct benefit, and some authors suggest that it provides better control of inflammation and improvement in cystoid macular edema. Vitrectomy is not reported as efficacious in cases of anterior uveitis, serpiginous chorioretinopathy, or Bartonella neuroretinitis.

pool.q: Detection of what antibody is most commonly associated with systemic granulomatosis with polyangiitis?
pool.rationale:
The antibody most commonly associated with systemic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is the antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) anti-proteinase 3, also known as c-ANCA.
Ribonucleoproteins are frequently encountered in mixed connective tissue diseases and Sjögren syndrome (SS). In SS, the anti-ribonucleoproteins include anti-SSA and anti-SSB. Anti-dsDNA antibodies can be found in systemic lupus erythematosus. The anti-ENAs are also associated with mixed connective tissue diseases.

pool.q: What feature characterizes West Nile virus retinopathy?

options.c: The virus can be transmitted to humans by mosquitoes.
options.d: The virus is a double-stranded DNA flavivirus.

pool.rationale: West Nile virus is typically transmitted to humans by mosquitoes. Retinopathy is an uncommon manifestation of the disease, which is caused by a single-stranded RNA flavivirus. The bird serves as the primary host. The retinitis is typically bilateral. Although there is no proven treatment, the disease is usually self-limited. The visual prognosis is favorable.

pool.q: What type of juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is associated with the highest risk of developing uveitis?
pool.rationale: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is classified into 5 types according to International League of Associations of Rheumatology (ILAR) guidelines. Oligoarticular onset, also known as pauciarticular onset, accounts for 80%-90% of patients with JIA-associated uveitis. Four or fewer joints are involved in the first 6 months of the disease. Ocular involvement is rare in systemic onset JIA. Polyarticular onset cases account for only 10% of JIA-associated uveitis. Enthesitis-related arthritis (ERA) is associated with a lower risk of uveitis than oligoarticular onset; however, uveitis in ERA patients is more likely to be acute and recurrent.

pool.q: What useful clinical feature suggests Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome?
pool.rationale: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome is associated with alopecia, vitiligo, and poliosis in about 30% of affected patients. It is more common in darkly pigmented ethnic groups and typically affects patients 30 to 50 years of age. It is not associated with skin hyperpigmentation. Additional occasionally useful features are headache, stiff neck, and meningismus.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 19-year-old patient with multiple sclerosis presents with floaters and blurred vision in the left eye. What finding is expected on ocular examination?
pool.rationale: Floaters and blurred vision are symptoms of intermediate uveitis, which may be associated with multiple sclerosis. Pain and redness are symptoms of anterior uveitis. Optic neuritis, despite being associated with multiple sclerosis, does not present with floaters.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient with Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome experienced resolution of bilateral serous retinal detachments with oral corticosteroid therapy. Six months later, the patient's visual acuity is 20/25 in both eyes. However, despite prednisolone acetate 1% drops every 2 hours and prednisone 20 mg/day orally, the patient is still plagued with persistent active anterior uveitis (2+ cells) in both eyes. What is the best next step in the treatment of this patient's condition?

options.a: Perform a vitrectomy to confirm the diagnosis.
options.b: Increase oral prednisone to 30 mg/day for the next 6 months.
options.d: Increase the frequency of topical corticosteroids to every 1 hour while maintaining 20 mg/day of prednisone for 6 more months.

pool.rationale:
Even though VKH syndrome is usually responsive to corticosteroid therapy, patients may experience recurrent episodes of inflammation. It is not safe nor recommended to use systemic corticosteroids on a long-term basis, so if there is recurrent inflammation, steroid-sparing immunomodulatory therapy should be considered.
VKH usually causes panuveitis, so topical therapy with corticosteroids will not be adequate.
The diagnosis of VKH is made on primarily clinical findings, so there is little confirmatory information to gain by performing diagnostic vitrectomy in this patient.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What feature is most consistent with uveitis in oligoarticular (also known as pauciarticular) juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA; formerly referred to as juvenile chronic arthritis and juvenile rheumatoid arthritis)?
pool.rationale: Indolent, bilateral, chronic anterior uveitis, characterized by a low-grade anterior chamber cellular reaction, is the most common ocular manifestation of oligoarticular JIA. Other manifestations of JIA-associated, chronic anterior uveitis include fine keratic precipitates, band keratopathy, posterior synechiae, cataracts, glaucoma, and macular edema. Intermediate uveitis with snowbanking is very rare in patients with JIA, and chorioretinal scars typically do not develop in these patients.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What would be the preferred management of a 12-year-old child who demonstrates the findings shown?
pool.rationale: This picture shows intraocular cysticercosis. Antihelminthic drugs can be helpful for neural cysticercosis, and a systemic evaluation is important, but antihelminthic drugs do not penetrate well into the eye. Laser can be helpful for small organisms under the retina, but larger and killed parasites can incite inflammation. The prognosis if untreated is poor, often with phthisis in 3–5 years. Surgical removal is the preferred treatment of this parasite. Antihelminthic medication (including albendazole) is useful for neurocysticercosis, but is not effective for ocular infection.

pool.q: A pseudophakic 52-year-old man complains of floaters and is found to have anterior chamber flare and cells in the anterior vitreous. He has a laser demarcation around an inferior retinal detachment. What is the most likely cause of his cell and flare?
pool.rationale:
Chronic peripheral rhegmatogenous retinal detachment can be associated with anterior segment cell and flare, along with vitreous cells. Patients often have good vision that can sometimes deteriorate because of cystoid macular edema (CME). Careful dilated fundus examination with scleral depression is of paramount importance in establishing the diagnosis. Findings may include peripheral pigment demarcation lines, subretinal fluid, retinal breaks, subretinal fibrosis, and peripheral retinal cysts.
Photoreceptor outer segments liberated from the subretinal space may be present in the anterior chamber, simulating inflammatory cells. In such situations, intraocular pressure (IOP) may be elevated, as these photoreceptor outer segments are phagocytosed by the endothelial cells in the trabecular meshwork, resulting in secondary open-angle glaucoma. This condition is called Schwartz syndrome; however, the condition is rare and specific to very anteriorized tears in the retina, involving the vitreous base, that give shed photoreceptor outer segments access to the anterior chamber (otherwise, with more posterior tears, photoreceptor outer segments would be trapped in the posterior segment by an intact hyaloid face).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What side effect is a known complication of intravitreal ganciclovir injections?
pool.rationale:
A known complication of intravitreal injections (as a whole, not just of ganciclovir) is retinal tear and detachment.
Intravitreal ganciclovir is not known to be associated with optic neuritis.
Although intravitreal injections of ganciclovir can transiently increase intraocular pressure, they are not associated with chronic glaucoma.
In addition to other antivirals (such as foscarnet and valganciclovir) that act on cytomegalovirus (CMV), the use of intravitreal ganciclovir may actually decrease the incidence of immune recovery uveitis, as opposed to promoting it. The exception to this rule is cidofovir, in which case the probability that a patient will develop immune recovery uveitis is significantly greater than in patients never having received this particular antiviral agent.
Additionally, 50% of patients with CMV retinitis and many other cases of viral retinitis may develop a retinal detachment during active disease or after successful treatment. Due to friability from retinal necrosis and multiple posterior holes, long-term silicone tamponade is often needed for surgical repair.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: When testing a patient with a suspected sarcoidosis, what invasive evaluation has the lowest yield (sensitivity) of confirming a diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
The most sensitive tests for detecting sarcoidosis are biopsy of a clinically apparent granuloma and computed tomography (CT) of the chest. However, biopsy of normal-appearing conjunctiva is very low yield.
In patients with suggestive chest imaging, bronchoalveolar lavage, and biopsy can be diagnostic, with a sensitivity approaching 90% for ultrasound-guided biopsy of pulmonary granulomas. Gallium scans may increase the sensitivity over plain chest radiography, but interpretation usually requires other confirmatory tests.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient with chronic anterior uveitis that is well controlled on topical prednisolone acetate 1% 4 times a day is found to have an intraocular pressure of 24 mm Hg in both eyes. There are 270 degrees of posterior synechiae. On gonioscopy, the angle is open. The optic nerve heads are without glaucomatous change. What is the next step in the management of this patient's condition?

options.b: performance of a peripheral iridectomy to prevent iris bombé
options.c: immediate discontinuation of topical corticosteroids and commencement of methotrexate
options.d: an attempt to taper topical corticosteroids

pool.rationale:
This patient has increased intraocular pressure due to use of topical corticosteroids. The angle is open without evidence of peripheral anterior synechiae, and there is no pupil block, so peripheral iridotomy is not indicated. Argon laser trabeculoplasty is usually not performed in uveitic glaucomas, in order to avoid exacerbating the uveitis.
Systemic immunosuppression with methotrexate can be offered if the topical steroids are ineffective. Uveitis is corticosteroid dependent and recurs every time corticosteroids are tapered, as well as if there are complications such as cystoid macular edema and secondary glaucoma.
In this situation, the topical corticosteroids can be gradually tapered, and in the meantime, topical anti–ocular-hypertensive agents can be employed if the raised intraocular pressure seems likely to cause harm. (It is doubtful in this case, because of non-glaucomatous optic nerves and mildly high IOP.)
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 40-year-old man complains of painless, progressive blurring of vision in one eye. Examination reveals a low-grade iritis, diffuse iris transillumination without posterior synechiae, and a 3+ posterior subcapsular cataract. There are diffuse stellate keratic precipitates. What is the best choice of preoperative treatment for cataract surgery in this patient?

options.a: Treatment should begin with topical prednisolone acetate 1% drops, every 2 hours, until the uveitis is quiet.
options.c: Treatment should begin with topical trifluridine 1% drops, 9 times a day, for 2 weeks, prior to surgery.
options.d: Treatment should begin with systemic prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks prior to surgery.

pool.rationale:
Fuchs uveitis syndrome (sometimes called Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis or Fuchs heterochromic uveitis) is unilateral, and symptoms can be overlooked. Blurry vision and discomfort are reported. Typically, patients have diffuse iris stromal atrophy leading to heterochromia, diffuse white stellate keratic precipitates, anterior chamber and anterior vitreous cells, or cataract. The diagnosis is usually based on heterochromia, distribution of the keratic precipitates, lack of posterior synechiae, and lack of symptoms.
The prognosis is good in most cases, although the inflammation can linger for years. Topical steroids can alleviate the inflammation, but typically do not resolve it. Aggressive treatment is not indicated in most of the cases.
These patients do quite well with cataract surgery and generally no preoperative treatment is needed.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 78-year-old pseudophakic man from a nursing home presented with severe pain and visual acuity of 20/100. He was diagnosed with endophthalmitis with culture showing streptococcal species. What part of this history portends a good prognosis?

options.b: relatively good visual acuity at presentation

pool.rationale:
Severe cases of endophthalmitis are correlated with loss of red fundus reflex, afferent pupillary defect, and poor vision at the time of initial presentation.
Lens status and living condition are not significant risk prognosticators.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 27-year-old woman has bilateral panuveitis, cavitary lung lesions, and kidney failure. What prophylactic measures should be considered before initiating definitive therapy with the most effective immunomodulatory treatment for this condition?
pool.rationale:
The patient in this clinical scenario has granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA). Of GPA patients treated with cyclophosphamide and corticosteroids, 93% successfully achieve remission.
Oocyte harvest and banking is prudent in a patient about to start cyclophosphamide who plans future pregnancies. Cyclophosphamide interferes with oogenesis and spermatogenesis. It may cause sterility in both sexes, and in some patients this may be irreversible. Other well-established adverse effects include teratogenicity, hemorrhagic cystitis, and development of secondary malignancies.
Variants in the gene encoding thiopurine S-methyltransferase (TPMT) alter its activity and may contribute to increased risk of hematologic events or leukopenia in treatment with thiopurines (eg, azathioprine), not cyclophosphamide.
Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scan/bone densitometry detects osteopenia/osteoporosis. It is useful in long-term corticosteroid administration, but osteopenia is not a significant risk of cyclophosphamide use.
Transesophageal echocardiogram detects cardiac and valvular structural abnormalities. Cardiac valve disease is not a significant risk of cyclophosphamide use, although acute cardiotoxicity has been reported in the setting of antineoplastic multi-drug therapy and transplant procedures involving this drug.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is a recommended therapy for Lyme disease?
pool.rationale: Doxycycline, ceftriaxone, amoxicillin, and cefuroxime are recommended when antibiotic treatment of Lyme disease is necessary. There is currently no FDA-approved vaccine for Lyme disease in the United States. Atovaquone is an anti-parasitic drug that is not used for Lyme disease.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Cyclosporine has been proven effective in controlled clinical studies for the treatment of what ocular inflammatory disease?

options.d: acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE)

pool.rationale:
Cyclosporine is a calcineurin inhibitor that eliminates T-cell receptor signal transduction, down-regulates interleukin-2 (IL-2) gene transcription and receptor expression of CD4+ T-lymphocytes. Cyclosporine has been shown to be effective in treating Behçet disease-associated uveitis in a randomized, controlled clinical trial; it provided control of inflammation in 50% of patients.
APMPPE usually does not require treatment; it is self-limited most of the time.
Immune recovery uveitis is anterior or intermediate uveitis, which presents when immune status improves with highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Usually, immune recovery uveitis is treated with local steroid therapy; systemic immunosuppressants are not indicated.
An infectious etiology should be ruled out in postsurgical scleritis before systemic immunosuppressants are used.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most appropriate treatment for  Lyme disease with papillitis?

options.a: oral cefuroxime with intravenous (IV) corticosteroids for 2 weeks
options.b: oral doxycycline with intravenous (IV) corticosteroids for 2 weeks
options.c: intravenous (IV) corticosteroids followed by oral taper

pool.rationale:
Stage 2, or disseminated, Lyme disease occurs a few weeks after exposure to spirochetes. The spirochetes spread to the skin, central nervous system (CNS), joints, heart, and eyes. The ocular disease in stage 2 includes anterior uveitis, intermediate uveitis, posterior uveitis, and panuveitis. These can be associated with granulomatous anterior uveitis, papillitis, choroiditis, vasculitis, and exudative retinal detachment.
Intraocular inflammation associated with Lyme disease, just like syphilis, is regarded as a manifestation of CNS disease. Patients require systemic (with oral amoxicillin or doxycycline; or intravenous ceftriaxone) antibiotic therapy. The routine use of systemic corticosteroids is still controversial, as antibiotic failures have been reported when corticosteroids are employed.
If corticosteroids are to be used to avoid a Jarisch-Herxheimer–like reaction, then oral (instead of intravenous) corticosteroids can be considered.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What form of uveitis is most likely to last less than 1 week?

options.d: acute anterior uveitis associated with Behçet disease

pool.rationale: Glaucomatocyclitic crisis (Posner-Schlossman syndrome) is characterized by recurrent unilateral hypertensive nongranulomatous anterior uveitis. This type of uveitis typically lasts less than 1 week. The other conditions listed are characterized by inflammation that lasts for longer than a week.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What should be the initial treatment of neovascularization of the disc in a patient with sarcoid-related panuveitis?

options.d: intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) inhibitors

pool.rationale:
Retinal neovascularization in uveitis results from chronic inflammation or capillary nonperfusion. Sarcoid panuveitis may be complicated with neovascularization of the disc and resolves completely with immunomodulatory and corticosteroid therapy alone.
Uveitides with retinal vasculitis may cause retinal neovascularization due to ischemia and thus may necessitate retinal laser photocoagulation or intravitreal anti-VEGF injection.
Treatment of subfoveal choroidal neovascularization (CNV) is accomplished with VEGF inhibitors; photodynamic therapy with verteporfin may be an adjunctive treatment.
In all cases, however, control of inflammation is paramount; this also reduces the risk of recurrence of CNV.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What antimetabolite is most commonly associated with hepatic toxicity?
pool.rationale: Although any antimetabolite can be associated with hepatic toxicity, methotrexate is most commonly associated with it. Often the elevation of liver enzyme levels is modest and reversible on holding the medication or decreasing the dose. Rarely, the liver damage can be severe and persistent, with resultant significant morbidity. Reversible hepatic toxicity occurs in 15% of patients on methotrexate, as opposed to 2% of patients taking azathioprine. Toxicity associated with azathioprine can be mitigated by assessing for thiopurine S-methyltransferase (TPMT) activity.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What percentage of all blindness in the United States is attributed to inadequately treated uveitis?
pool.rationale: Worldwide, ocular inflammatory disease is a significant cause of low vision and blindness. In the United States, 10% of all blindness is attributed to inadequately treated uveitis.

pool.q: Three weeks ago, a 78-year-old man tripped and fell on a sidewalk and his right eye was perforated by the tooth of a rake. He has a 360-degree dense subconjunctival hemorrhage, an intraocular pressure of 8, and a peaked pupil. The left eye has the appearance shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: The attached photo is significant for granulomatous keratic precipitates. Sympathetic ophthalmia is a bilateral granulomatous uveitis that occurs after trauma to one of the eyes. A septic endophthalmitis would not be expected in the nontraumatized eye. Sarcoidosis and Lyme disease can also cause granulomatous uveitis, though those diagnoses are less likely in this scenario.

pool.q: A patient with AIDS presents with bilateral yellow, placoid retinal lesions. What is the best initial testing to perform and best initial treatment?

options.a: Check CD4+ helper T lymphocyte count and start systemic corticosteroids.
options.b: Check rapid plasmin reagin and start intramuscular benzathine penicillin G, 2.4 million U, as a single dose.
options.c: Check CD4+ helper T lymphocyte count and start antiretroviral therapy.
options.d: Check rapid plasmin reagin and start intravenous penicillin G, 18-24 million U, administered daily for 10 days.

pool.rationale:
Syphilis may occur as a coinfection in HIV-affected individuals. Syphilis in such patients may present as placoid lesions, as described in this case. Thus, suspicion for syphilis should be high in this patient and checking the rapid plasmin reagin (RPR) will help assess response to treatment. Ocular cases of syphilis should be treated in the same manner as neurosyphilis. Thus, intravenous penicillin G 18-24 million units for 10-14 days is indicated. Syphilis without neurologic or ocular involvement may be treated intramuscularly as a single dose.
Checking CD4+ helper T lymphocyte count and starting antiretroviral therapy would be an ideal option if the patient exhibited features only of HIV retinopathy (cotton-wool spots, microaneurysms, and retinal hemorrhages). Systemic corticosteroids may be used in treating immune recovery uveitis, which occurs in the setting of prior CMV retinitis. However, systemic steroids may be used if there is a prominent inflammatory reaction in syphilis. The use of systemic steroids, however, should only occur after treatment with intravenous penicillin has commenced.

pool.q: What dosage of oral prednisone is considered to be the threshold for increasing toxicity that can induce osteoporosis?
pool.rationale: The risk of osteoporosis is higher for postmenopausal women and men older than 50 years who take ≥7.5 mg/day of prednisone or its equivalent for longer than 3 months. To lessen the risk, patients receiving long-term corticosteroid maintenance therapy should supplement their diets with calcium and vitamin D, except with certain medications; the advice of the physician prescribing those drugs should be obtained.

pool.q: A patient presents with acute anterior uveitis and decreased vision. The patient denies pain with eye movements. Pupillary function is normal without afferent pupillary defect. Color plates are full. Anterior segment findings include 2+ diffuse perilimbal injection, 3+ anterior chamber cell, 1+ flare, and a clear crystalline lens. Dilated fundoscopic examination shows hyperemia of the optic nerve and a blunted foveal reflex, but no vitritis or chorioretinal lesions. What test would most likely demonstrate the cause of decreased vision in this case?

options.a: optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula
options.b: optical coherence tomography of the optic nerve
options.c: B-scan ultrasonography of the optic nerve

pool.rationale:
The cause of the patient's decreased vision would best be discerned through OCT of the macula, as it is not uncommon for inflammatory cytokines associated with acute anterior uveitis to diffuse posteriorly and result in swelling of the optic nerve head and in cystoid macular edema (CME).
It is important to understand that the presence of optic nerve and retinal edema alone are not synonymous with posterior uveitis or optic neuritis. Optic nerve and retinal edema occur in many processes including anterior uveitis, intermediate uveitis, posterior uveitis, panuveitis. Edema can also occur in unrelated entities such as hypotony maculopathy in the setting of an overfiltering bleb in glaucoma patients. To further clarify that the optic nerve head hyperemia in this patient is not indicative of an optic neuritis or posterior uveitis, the question stem not only states that this is an acute anterior uveitis, but also explains that there is no pain with eye movements, no vitritis, no chorioretinitis, no afferent pupillary defect, and full color plate testing. Another option to ensure that optic nerve function is normal could be to perform a visual field, which should either be full in the absence of other pathology or show a possible enlarged blind spot from the edema at the nerve head. Therefore, OCT and/or B-scan ultrasonography of the optic nerve head will not be as helpful in this scenario, as there is no reason to suspect an optic neuritis or posterior scleritis with associated optic nerve swelling in this case.
ERG may be helpful in conditions primarily involving the retina or choroid, such as certain white dot syndromes or birdshot retinochoroidopathy, but not in the setting of acute anterior uveitis where optic nerve head edema and macular edema can result from posterior diffusion of inflammatory cytokines.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What symptom(s) characterize(s) the presentation of serpiginous choroiditis?

options.b: gradual loss of vision with pain and photophobia
options.c: sudden profound complete loss of vision
options.d: sudden onset of central or paracentral scotoma

pool.rationale: Serpiginous choroiditis, also termed geographic or helicoid choroidopathy, is likely inflammatory, but it typically does not manifest with significant vitreous or anterior segment inflammation. Because of this, floaters and photophobia are not cardinal symptoms. The onset of symptoms is relatively sudden with a painless, unilateral, paracentral scotoma and potentially decreased vision, but it may proceed asymmetrically and with intermittent periods of progression. Many patients progress to vision of 20/200 or worse with involvement of the macula, but this decline in visual acuity typically develops over months or years. Patients may require aggressive anti-inflammatory treatment and need to be followed closely for the development of choroidal neovascularization and progression of disease. Tuberculosis-associated disease should be considered in the differential diagnosis.

pool.q: What test is most appropriate in the initial workup of a patient with uveitis suspected of having sarcoidosis?
pool.rationale:
Chest x-ray is the single best screening modality for patients suspected of having sarcoidosis, as it reveals abnormalities in approximately 90% of patients who have sarcoidosis. The classic feature of a chest x-ray (CXR) in this setting is hilar lymphadenopathy, although chest computed tomography (CT) may also reveal mediastinal and other parenchymal abnormalities. Although retinal angiography may reveal leakage from retinal vasculitis (technically, retinal phlebitis), retinal vasculitis is not specific to sarcoidosis and can be seen in several other posterior uveitides. ANA and CRP have no screening value for patients suspected of having sarcoidosis.
Chest abnormalities are present at some point in up to 90% of sarcoid patients, but these do not persist throughout the disease course and thus maybe absent at the time of workup. High resolution chest computed tomography is more sensitive imaging modality and may be particularly valuable in patients with a normal appearance on CXR, but for whom a high clinical index of suspicion remains; the risk of increased radiation must be weighed against the clinical utility of the information gained in such cases.

pool.q: What is the most effective treatment for preventing sympathetic ophthalmia (SO) in the fellow eye after a penetrating trauma that resulted in "no light perception" vision in the traumatized eye?

options.a: prompt systemic prednisone at the time of the initial trauma
options.b: immunosuppressive therapy within 2 weeks of the initial trauma
options.c: repair of the open ocular wounds within 24 hours

pool.rationale:
SO is a bilateral, granulomatous panuveitis that may develop after trauma or surgery in 1 eye. After a latency period, the uninjured fellow eye (sympathizing eye) develops panuveitis. Until recently, accidental penetrating ocular trauma was the most common precipitating event. Vitreoretinal surgery has now become the main risk for developing SO.
Every attempt should be made to repair the injury and close the ocular wounds, as soon as possible. However, if the eye is grossly disorganized, with no possible salvage, then enucleation within 2 weeks of injury may prevent the development of SO.
Systemic steroids and immunosuppressive therapy are indicated for the initial treatment of SO once the condition is present. However, prophylactic steroids and immunosuppressive therapy have not been shown to prevent the development of SO.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What systemic medical condition is associated with acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE)?
pool.rationale:
Although APMPPE typically occurs in otherwise healthy adults, systemic conditions should be considered. Cerebral vasculitis can be a complicating comorbid condition, and syphilis may masquerade with an indistinguishable fundus appearance.
Rheumatoid arthritis is the most common autoimmune disease associated with scleritis or peripheral ulcerative keratitis.
MS has been associated with many types of ocular inflammation but optic neuritis and intermediate uveitis are most typical.
Central nervous system lymphoma may present with intraocular lymphoma; the subretinal and vitreous aggregates of lymphoid cells may share features of APMPPE at first, but typically affect much older patients, and are progressive—both uncharacteristic of APMPPE.

pool.q: For a patient less than 6 years old with unilateral pseudohypopyon, what is the primary concern when considering an aqueous or vitreous aspirate?

options.a: risk of vitreous wicking and/or cataractogenesis
options.c: risk of dispersing malignant retinoblastoma cells

pool.rationale: Retinoblastoma, especially the variant of diffuse infiltrating retinoblastoma, may present with anterior chamber cells, pseudohypopyon that shifts with change of head position, or vitreous opacity and other signs of inflammation, but lack the typical calcification usually seen with this tumor. Aspiration can be diagnostic, but it carries the risk of seeding the tumor via the needle or surgical track. The risks of general anesthesia and direct complications of diagnostic aspiration, such as cataract formation and sympathetic ophthalmia, are low; thus, if definitive diagnosis and subsequent management necessitates obtaining an aspirate, benefits would outweigh risks.

pool.q: A 52-year-old white woman presents with decreased vision. The fundoscopic examination image is shown. What treatment should be initiated?

options.b: no treatment (most patients will retain good vision without it)
options.c: isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol daily
options.d: systemic and/or local corticosteroids with early introduction of corticosteroid-sparing immunomodulatory therapy

pool.rationale:
The fundus photos show birdshot retinochoroidopathy (vitiliginous chorioretinitis). This is a relatively uncommon disease that is classically found in white women of northern European descent, 40 years and older. There is no known systemic association with this disease. Birdshot retinochoroidopathy has a high correlation with the HLA-A29 haplotype, which has a sensitivity of 96% and a specificity of 93%, according to the Basic and Clinical Science Course. The fundoscopic examination of birdshot retinochoroidopathy shows characteristic multifocal, hypopigmented, ovoid, cream-colored lesions at the level of the choroid and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Patients present with decreased vision, nyctalopia, floaters, or disturbed color vision. Electroretinography and visual field testing are useful in following disease course and response to therapy. Without treatment, few patients maintain good vision.
Typical treatment consists initially of systemic corticosteroids, with immunomodulatory medications for adjunct and maintenance therapy (methotrexate, cyclosporine, etc.). Periocular steroid can also be useful in treatment for cystoid macular edema (CME), on the complications of birdshot retinochoroidopathy.
Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol are used to treat tuberculosis, which may mimic a serpiginous choroiditis. Intravitreal ganciclovir may be used to treat herpes simplex virus-associated chorioretinitis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A positive result on an indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA) or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for Borrelia burgdorferi in a patient with intermediate uveitis should prompt what action as the most appropriate next step?

options.a: confirmation of serological results with a Western blot
options.c: comparison of titer to standard curve to determine bacterial load
options.d: institution of intravenous penicillin for 10 to 14 days

pool.rationale:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends a 2-step protocol for the diagnosis of active or previous infection with Borrelia burgdorferi: ELISA for immunoglobulin M (IgM) and IgG, and if this result is positive, then Western immunoblot testing.
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based testing can also be used.
For patients with only ocular involvement (ie, without CNS or cardiac involvement), the route and duration of antibiotic treatment is not well established.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What animal model of uveitis most closely resembles Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome in humans?
pool.rationale: VKH is a bilateral granulomatous panuveitis in humans. Of the choices listed, only experimental autoimmune uveoretinitis induces a panuveitis. Equine recurrent uveitis can produce vitreal involvement, but it is mainly an anterior uveitis. AIRE (for autoimmune regulator) is a transcription factor used by the thymus in the process of establishing thymic tolerance. Early in life, the thymus expresses many cell-type–specific proteins; T‑cell clones reactive to these proteins are deleted. This mechanism is important in the development of self-tolerance. Mice deficient in AIRE do not express these proteins during development; thus, autoreactive T cells escape deletion, and the mice spontaneously develop a posterior uveitis. Endotoxin-induced (also termed experimental immune) uveitis (EIU) is a transient uveitis model induced by footpad, intraperitoneal, or intravitreal injection of lipopolysaccharide in mice and rats.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most appropriate indication for chorioretinal biopsy?

options.a: bilateral heavy vitritis with subretinal infiltrates in a 75-year-old male
options.b: diffuse unilateral vitritis in a 4-year-old child with concurrent esotropia
options.c: acute onset of diffuse, unilateral, peripheral retinal whitening and vascular sheathing in a 36-year-old female
options.d: sight-threatening chorioretinitis with negative workup that is nonresponsive to therapy

pool.rationale:
When diagnostic workup, as in the case of sight-threatening chorioretinitis, fails to reveal a diagnosis or, at the very least distinguish between noninfectious, infectious, or masquerade (eg, malignant) etiologies, a chorioretinal biopsy can be considered, since this will biopsy the tissue directly involved.
In the case of a diffuse unilateral vitritis in a 4-year-old child, vitreous aspiration or vitrectomy is more appropriate, especially considering that this is the primary site of involvement. The case of bilateral heavy vitritis with subretinal infiltrates is suspicious for a masquerade syndrome (namely primary vitreoretinal lymphoma), and in such cases a vitrectomy can be both diagnostic and therapeutic. Ancillary tests could be considered in such cases, and assays for IL-10 and IL-6 levels (from vitreous or aqueous) could be included.
An acute, diffuse, unilateral peripheral retinal whitening with vascular sheathing is consistent with acute retinal necrosis. In this setting, vitreous (or aqueous) aspiration should be considered to evaluate for herpetic etiologies (including herpes simplex virus [HSV]-1/2, varicella zoster virus [VZV], or, in immunocompromised patients, cytomegalovirus [CMV]) via polymerase chain reaction (PCR).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the typical ophthalmoscopic finding in multifocal choroiditis with panuveitis?

options.a: geographic chorioretinal pigmented scars radiating from the optic nerve
options.b: choroidal infiltrates larger than 1 disc diameter
options.c: small white choroidal lesions (200-500 µm) that resolve spontaneously over 4-8 weeks
options.d: small creamy lesions acutely that become punched out over time

pool.rationale: The inflammatory lesions in multifocal choroiditis may vary somewhat in number, appearance, and location, but they are rarely larger than 1500 μm, evolve into punched-out atrophic scars, and are associated with at least some degree of vitreous and sometimes anterior chamber inflammation. The lesions associated with birdshot retinochoroidopathy are often arranged in a radiating pattern centered on the optic nerve.

pool.q: When stellate keratic precipitates are present in herpes simplex type 1 intraocular infections, how are they typically distributed on the corneal endothelium?

options.a: in the inferior third of the cornea (Arlt triangle)
options.d: keratic precipitates are not found in herpes simplex type 1 intraocular infections

pool.rationale: Stellate keratic precipitates (KPs) are very suggestive of a viral intraocular infection and are frequently seen. However, in herpetic intraocular infections, particularly with herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2 as well as varicella-zoster virus, there may be nongranulomatous or granulomatous KPs as well. In this question, stellate KPs are identified and, when present, often are found diffusely. The KPs localizing only to the inferior third of the cornea (Arlt triangle) are classically found in noninfectious etiologies of intraocular inflammation and may be either granulomatous or nongranulomatous. Coin-shaped lesions are found in cytomegalovirus anterior uveitis.
