pool.q: At a minimum, most uveitis specialists will employ what study in the workup of ocular inflammation in an immunocompetent patient?
pool.rationale:
There is no single, standardized battery of tests to be ordered for all patients with uveitis. It is important to rule out an underlying systemic or infectious disease. At a minimum, it might be worthwhile to order a few tests based on the assessment of uveitis questionnaire.
Complementary investigations for uveitis should be guided by a pretest probability of etiology, the ophthalmic signs and symptoms, and therapeutic consequences.
Syphilis is one of great masqueraders of medicine and should always be considered in the differential diagnosis of any intraocular inflammatory disease.
The prevalence of lupus is less than 0.47% in patients with uveitis, so the positive predictive value of antinuclear antibodies (ANA) for the diagnosis is less than 3%. Therefore, checking ANA titers is rarely useful.
ESR and C-reactive protein are nonspecific, so are rarely helpful in finding an etiology.
Tests for tuberculosis are routinely considered in the "essential" workup; however, if an immunocompetent patient with uveitis is from an area where tuberculosis is not endemic, has a reliable travel history, and has had no exposure to other people with tuberculosis, TB testing would have a low yield.
An HLA-B27 should be considered for patients in the pertinent demographic and who have an appropriate presentation, but HLA-B27 would not be the first choice for a "minimal" workup.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: For patients in the early course of birdshot retinochoroidopathy, what is the most common cause of decreased central visual acuity?
pool.rationale: Vitreous opacities, cataract, RPE atrophy, and CME can characterize birdshot retinochoroidopathy. However, CME is the most common cause of decreased central visual acuity in birdshot, with one study noting 50.5% of cases having CME as the most common cause of visual loss. Recall that CME is the most frequent cause of vision loss in general in uveitic patients. Cataract would be expected to develop either if the inflammation is not controlled or if frequent and chronic topical, periocular, or high-dose systemic corticosteroids are employed. Vitreous haze can develop in birdshot, though it is rarely significant enough to affect visual acuity. RPE atrophy, in addition to optic nerve pallor and vascular attenuation, is a late manifestation of the disease.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A new patient presents for assessment of uveitis with a calcific band in the interpalpebral zone. What does that tell you about the patient's uveitis?
pool.rationale: Calcific band keratopathy develops in patients with chronic uveitis over years. It is not specifically associated with sarcoidosis or anterior uveitis and is not painful.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the causative organism of iris gummas?
pool.rationale:
Treponema pallidum

Gummas (or gummata) are the characteristic lesions of benign tertiary syphilis. The ocular manifestations of syphilis are protean and may affect all structures in the eye. Syphilitic iridocyclitis may be associated with iris roseola, iris papulosa, iris nodosa, and iris gummata. Syphilis is a spirochete infection caused by Treponema pallidum.
Baylisascaris procyonis is a raccoon roundworm causing diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis. Borrelia burgdorferi causes Lyme disease, and Bartonella henselae is the causative agent of cat-scratch disease.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common cause of vision loss due to ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (OHS)?
pool.rationale:
The most common cause of vision loss in OHS is CNV. If 1 eye with OHS has CNV, then the risk that the other eye will develop visual loss is 1% if there are no findings of OHS in the fellow eye; 4% if there is peripapillary atrophy in the fellow eye; and 25% if focal macular histo spots are present. The treatment of CNV in OHS includes photodynamic therapy or anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy.
Inflammatory vitreous opacities and retinal vasculitis are absent in OHS. The classic peripheral punched-out chorioretinal scars of OHS typically do not cause vision loss.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: For an AIDS patient that has the fundus findings shown, what is the most likely symptom that he might experience?
pool.rationale: The image represents peripheral "granular" cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis. Typical features include minimal or no vitreous inflammation, preservation of the vessels (although varying amounts of vasculitis/sheathing may be present), and steady progression without treatment. Because the lesions are usually peripheral and the host immune response is compromised, signs or symptoms such as pain, redness, and decreased vision are scarce; thus, routine screening ophthalmoscopy is recommended for those with CD4+ T-cell counts below 250 cells/μL.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 32-year-old woman reports one week of floaters in her left eye. She denies flashes of light or sudden trauma. On examination, the ophthalmologist notices a mild anterior chamber reaction and peripheral snowballs and snowbanks in the affected eye. What tests would be most appropriate to order?

options.a: HLA-B27, rapid plasma reagin (RPR), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
options.b: Lyme titers, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and rapid plasma reagin (RPR)
options.c: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), Toxoplasma IgG and IgM, and Lyme titers
options.d: Toxoplasma IgG and IgM, serum angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE), and rapid plasma reagin (RPR)

pool.rationale: The findings noted suggest pars planitis. The differential diagnosis for this includes sarcoidosis, syphilis, toxocariasis, lyme disease, multiple sclerosis, and tuberculosis. Toxoplasmosis does not cause pars planitis, nor does HLA-B27-associated uveitis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In what part of the eye does endogenous fungal endophthalmitis typically begin?
pool.rationale: The infection usually begins in the choroid, appearing as yellow-white lesions with indistinct borders that range in size from small cotton-wool spots to several disc diameters. It can subsequently break through into the vitreous, producing localized cellular and fungal aggregates overlying the original site. Iris nodules and rubeosis may also be observed in cases of severe fungal endophthalmitis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Progressive outer retinal necrosis may be distinguished from acute retinal necrosis by the presence of what feature?

options.b: polymerase chain reaction (PCR) positive for herpes simplex
options.c: patchy areas of outer retinal whitening

pool.rationale: The essential difference between progressive outer retinal necrosis (PORN) and acute retinal necrosis (ARN) is the presence of an intact immune function in ARN. Both PORN and ARN are typically caused by herpes family viruses, specifically herpes simplex types 1 and 2, and the herpes zoster or varicella virus. Goldmann-Witmer coefficient together with PCR increase the yield of diagnosing viral infections. The HLA-A29 genotype is associated with birdshot chorioretinopathy, and has not been reported in relation to viral retinitis. While HLA Aw33 phenotype has been reported to increase the relative risk of developing ARN in Japanese patients.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Three weeks after bowel surgery, a patient presents with 2+ anterior chamber cells, 2+ vitreous cells, vitreal haze with snowball-like condensations, and a small white retinal lesion in 1 eye. He had been in the intensive care unit on parenteral nutrition for a week. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Candida albicans endophthalmitis

Patients receiving parenteral nutrition are at risk for developing fungal infections that can become hematogenously disseminated, thereby resulting in Candida endophthalmitis. Candida is the most common organism causing endogenous endophthalmitis. Candida endophthalmitis will typically present as fluffy, round vitreous opacities in addition to creamy white chorioretinal lesions.
IBD with uveitis typically presents in a patient with IBD symptoms, and this noninfectious uveitis typically presents in a recurrent nongranulomatous manner.
The ocular inflammation in sarcoidosis may present as a granulomatous uveitis and can affect anterior, intermediate, or posterior segments, or be panuveitic in nature.
The classic features of ocular sarcoidosis include mutton-fat keratic precipitates (KPs), Busacca and Koeppe nodules, vitreous snowballs (string of pearls presentation is characteristic), "candlewax dripping" vasculitis, and choroidal and optic nerve nodules (which have been shown to represent granulomas).
The uveitis caused by Tropheryma whipplei can present as panuveitis or retinal vasculitis; this entity should be suspected in patients with abdominal pain, diarrhea or steatorrhea, weight loss, and neurologic dysfunction.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What intraocular infection is most commonly associated with immune recovery uveitis in a patient with AIDS whose immune function has improved with antiretroviral therapy?
pool.rationale: Immune recovery uveitis is observed in patients with previous CMV retinitis and recovered immune systems, most often in patients with AIDS who have received antiretroviral therapy. CMV retinitis is usually associated with a minimal inflammatory response in AIDS patients; the inflammation of immune recovery uveitis is presumably the reconstituted immune system’s response to CMV antigens.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Progressive outer retinal necrosis (PORN) syndrome is most commonly associated with what virus?
pool.rationale:
PORN syndrome is a variant of herpetic viral retinitis seen in HIV-infected patients. Initially, PORN may be difficult to differentiate from CMV retinitis, but rapid progression distinguishes varicella-zoster or herpes simplex from CMV infections.
Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis can mimic PORN in AIDS patients, and vitreous polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is often required to differentiate the possible etiologies.
Bartonella species may cause bacillary angiomatosis or neuroretinitis but are not associated with a peripheral retinitis.
The human papillomavirus (HPV) is associated with cervical and squamous carcinoma but has no known association with retinitis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What neurological complication is most commonly seen with Borrelia burgdorferi infection?
pool.rationale: The most common neuro-ophthalmologic manifestation of Lyme disease is seventh cranial nerve palsy (Bell palsy). It may be unilateral or bilateral. Other cranial nerve palsies have been reported, and Horner syndrome may be associated but is uncommon. Optic nerve swelling (papillitis) and neuroretinitis are also associated with Lyme disease.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Histoplasma capsulatum infection most commonly occurs in what geographic area?
pool.rationale: The highest prevalence of H capsulatum exposure is in the Mississippi and Ohio River watersheds. Although the Missouri River is a branch of the Mississippi, H capsulatum has not been found endemic to its valley. Coccidioidomycosis, which can be found in the San Joaquin Valley as well as in the soil of several southwestern states, Mexico, and Central and South America, may mimic the clinical features of presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome ("punched-out" small chorioretinal scars, peripapillary scarring). This disorder is due to the fungus Coccidioides, not H capsulatum. The Hudson River valley is devoid of H capsulatum.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the definitive treatment for a patient with phacolytic uveitis?

options.a: topical prednisolone acetate drops given hourly
options.b: oral methotrexate following baseline hepatic function tests

pool.rationale: An immune reaction to lens material may result in ocular inflammatory disease. This reaction may follow disruption of the lens capsule (traumatic or surgical), termed phacoantigenic uveitis, or leakage of lens protein through the intact lens capsule in mature or hypermature cataracts, termed phacolytic uveitis. While antiinflammatory medications may be used to reduce inflammation, the definitive treatment is to remove the inciting lens material.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Methotrexate produces its anti-inflammatory effect by what mechanism of action?
pool.rationale: Methotrexate, a folic acid analogue and inhibitor of dihydrofolate reductase, inhibits DNA replication, but its anti-inflammatory effects result from extracellular release of adenosine.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the treatment for visually significant calcific band keratopathy?
pool.rationale: Not all band keratopathy needs to be treated, but if it is symptomatic or visually significant, the treatment is epithelial debridement followed by chelation with ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What disease is typically treated with an intravitreal antiviral medication?
pool.rationale:
Acute retinal necrosis is a kind of necrotizing herpetic retinopathy. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based assays have shown that the most common cause of ARN is varicella zoster virus (VZV), followed by herpes simplex virus (HSV)-1, HSV-2, and rarely cytomegalovirus (CMV). High-dose systemic oral or intravenous antiviral therapy alone or in combination with intravitreal antivirals is indicated for treatment of this sight-threatening condition.
An infectious cause has not been proven for MEWDS, Behçet disease, nor VKH, so antivirals are not usually employed for those conditions.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What test is indicated periodically in patients being treated with azathioprine for eye disease with no systemic symptoms?
pool.rationale:
Azathioprine is an oral antimetabolite that is often used to treat ocular inflammatory diseases, such as uveitis and mucous membrane pemphigoid. Hepatotoxicity and blood cell dyscrasias are the most common adverse effects that would be detected by screening laboratory studies; thus, most surveillance regimens include getting a complete blood cell count. Liver enzymes, such as ALT, should be checked before initiating therapy, within 1 to 2 weeks after initiating therapy, and regularly thereafter.
Use of the alkylating agent cyclophosphamide can result in hemorrhagic cystitis. Consumption of adequate water is therefore recommended when taking this drug, and urinalysis is indicated. Cyclosporine and tacrolimus are more typically associated with nephrotoxicity, and screening blood pressure measurements and serum creatinine are indicated.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What medication is best used as an intravitreal injection in the treatment of cytomegalovirus retinitis?
pool.rationale: Foscarnet and ganciclovir are medications appropriate as intravitreal preparations for the treatment of CMV retinitis. Of the choices listed here, foscarnet is the best. Valganciclovir is the L-valyl ester prodrug of ganciclovir. The valine increases both the absorption of the drug in the intestines and the bioavailability of the drug once it is absorbed. Cidofovir was previously used as intravitreal therapy for the treatment of CMV, especially in the pre-highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) era, but this medication is associated with hypotonous uveitis, which can lead to blindness. Acyclovir is not appropriate for CMV, because acyclovir needs to be phosphorylated by a viral thymidine kinase (TK) and CMV lacks TK

pool.q: What infectious organism is mostly likely to cause chorioretinitis adjacent to a chorioretinal scar?
pool.rationale: The most common cause of chorioretinitis is toxoplasmosis. Toxoplasmosis often recurs adjacent to scars indicating a prior episode, but it can also occur at "de novo" locations in the fundus. Acute retinal necrosis (usually secondary to herpes simplex virus or varicella zoster virus) and cytomegalovirus retinitis are not likely to be associated with pre-existing scars. Congenital rubella syndrome may cause diffuse retinal pigment epithelial mottling but is not classically associated with a pre-existing chorioretinal scar.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An 18-year-old woman presents with floaters and decreased vision in both eyes. Examination reveals vitreous cells, snowbanking, and cystoid macular edema OU. What systemic disease is this patient at greatest risk of developing?
pool.rationale: Multiple sclerosis is known to develop in 15% of young patients who present with idiopathic intermediate uveitis (pars planitis). CNS lymphoma is largely a disease of the elderly and should be considered in elderly patients who present with idiopathic vitritis. Refsum disease is an autosomal recessive phytanic acid storage disease that presents with a pigmentary retinopathy and reduced electroretinogram (ERG) signals, cerebellar ataxia, polyneuropathy, anosmia, hearing loss, and cardiomyopathy, but not vitritis or intermediate uveitis. Sarcoidosis can masquerade as any form of uveitis but is characterized as a granulomatous anterior or panuveitis rather than an isolated intermediate uveitis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient has parotitis, fever, facial nerve palsy, and uveitis. What disease is the patient most likely to have?
pool.rationale:
Systemic sarcoidosis may present acutely, frequently with associated anterior uveitis in young patients. One form of acute sarcoidosis, called Löfgren syndrome, consists of erythema nodosum, febrile arthropathy, bilateral hilar adenopathy, and acute iritis and is quite responsive to systemic corticosteroids; it has a good long-term prognosis. Another, termed Heerfordt syndrome (uveoparotid fever), is characterized by uveitis, parotitis, fever, and facial nerve palsy. Chronic sarcoidosis presents insidiously and is characterized by persistent disease of more than 2 years’ duration, frequently with interpulmonary involvement and chronic uveitis. Extended corticosteroid therapy may be required. Pulmonary disease is the major cause of morbidity; overall mortality from sarcoidosis approaches 5% but may be as high as 10% with neurosarcoidosis.
Systemic lupus, myasthenia gravis, and Behçet disease do not present with this clinical picture.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is a helpful diagnostic characteristic of multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (shown)?
pool.rationale: Multiple evanescent white dot syndrome is usually unilateral. It is most common in young females, not males. The tempo of onset is typically rapid or explosive. The associated peripapillary, central, or cecocentral scotomata usually resolve over several weeks. Recurrence is uncommon.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Uveitis & Ocular Inflammation — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most appropriate treatment for Pneumocystis jirovecii choroiditis?
pool.rationale:
Patients with AIDS are at greater risk than the general population for P jirovecii pneumonia. In rare cases, this infection can result in choroidal infiltrates that contain the microorganisms. P jirovecii can present as choroiditis that consists of slightly elevated, plaquelike, yellow-white lesions located in the choroid, with minimal vitritis. On fluorescein angiography, these lesions tend to be hypofluorescent in the early phase and hyperfluorescent in the later phases. If disseminated P jirovecii infection is suspected, an extensive examination by an infectious disease specialist is required.
Treatment of P jirovecii choroiditis involves a 3-week regimen of intravenous trimethoprim (20 mg/kg/day) and sulfamethoxazole (100 mg/kg/day) or pentamidine (4 mg/kg/day). Within 3–12 weeks, most of the yellow-white lesions disappear, leaving mild overlying pigmentary changes. Vision is usually not affected.

pool.q: Why do autoimmune regulator (AIRE)–deficient mice develop spontaneous uveitis?

options.a: Retinal antigens are overexpressed in regional lymph nodes.
options.b: Complement regulatory molecules are absent in the eyes of these animals.
options.d: The CD4:CD8 T helper cell ratio is reversed compared with that in wild type mice.

pool.rationale: AIRE is a transcription factor used by the thymus in the process of establishing thymic tolerance. Early in life, the thymus expresses many cell-type–specific proteins; T-cell clones reactive to these proteins are deleted. This mechanism is important in the development of self-tolerance. Mice deficient in AIRE do not express these proteins during development; thus, autoreactive T cells escape deletion, and the mice spontaneously develop a posterior uveitis.

pool.q: By what mechanism does cyclosporine treat uveitis?

options.a: inhibits T-cell receptor signal transduction and downregulates interleukin-2 (IL-2) activity
options.b: directly inhibits tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) as a fully human monoclonal immunoglobulin G1 (IgG1) antibody against TNF-α
options.c: inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and DNA replication, and causes extracellular release of adenosine
options.d: alkylates purines in DNA and RNA causing abnormal DNA replication and cell death

pool.rationale:
Types of immunomodulatory therapy (IMT), also known as immunosuppressive or disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), are often divided into nonbiologic-IMT and biologic agents. Cyclosporine is a nonbiologic-IMT, and furthermore is a T-cell inhibitor, which is so-called due to its mechanism of action. Cyclosporine inhibits T-cells by inhibiting calcineurin, which then stops T-cell receptor signal transduction (T-cell signaling), and downregulates interleukin-2 (IL-2) activity. IL-2 is downregulated due to decreased IL-2 gene transcription and receptor expression of CD4+ lymphocytes. Tacrolimus is the other T-cell inhibitor or calcineurin inhibitor that is used for uveitis treatment.
The other answers describe mechanisms of action (MOA) of other non-biologic and biologic IMT medications. Beside T-cell inhibitors, nonbiologic-IMT medications also include antimetabolites and alkylating agents. Biologic agents are genetically engineered proteins targeting specific immune processes, and they include tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) inhibitors and inhibitors of others proinflammatory mediators.
The answer choice "inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and DNA replication, and causes extracellular release of adenosine" describes the MOA of methotrexate, which is an antimetabolite. It is a folic acid analogue and dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor. It reduces DNA replication, but the anti-inflammatory mechanism occurs due to extracellular release of adenosine. The other antimetabolites used to treat uveitis include azathioprine, which is a purine nucleoside analogue that interferes with DNA replication and RNA transcription, and mycophenolate mofetil, which inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase and DNA replication.
The answer choice "alkylates purines in DNA and RNA causing abnormal DNA replication and cell death" describes the MOA of cyclophosphamide, which is an alkylating agent. It alkylates purines in DNA and RNA, causing impaired DNA replication and cell death. The other alkylating agent used to treat uveitis is chlorambucil, which also interferes with DNA replication. Cyclophosphamide and chlorambucil are typically reserved for severe, vision-threatening, or life-threatening inflammation that other less toxic therapies failed to manage.
The answer choice "directly inhibits tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) as a fully human monoclonal immunoglobulin G1 (IgG1) antibody against TNF-α" describes the MOA of the biologic agent adalimumab, which is a TNF-α inhibitor. It is a fully human monoclonal immunoglobulin G1 (IgG1) antibody that targets TNF-α. It was the first FDA-approved systemic medication for noninfectious uveitis. The other TNF-α inhibitor that is used for uveitis treatment currently is infliximab. It is a mouse/human chimeric immunoglobulin G1 kappa (KgG1κ) monoclonal antibody against TNF-α.
Within the category of biologic agents, besides TNF-α inhibitors, there are also others including rituximab, which is a chimeric monoclonal antibody against CD20+ cells (mostly B lymphocytes), interferon alpha-2a/2b (IFN-α2a/2b), which has antiviral, immunomodulatory, and antiangiogenic effects, and abatacept, which inhibits T-cell costimulation.

pool.q: A 54-year-old white woman presents with floaters, photopsia, and nyctalopia of several months' duration. On examination, visual acuity is 20/20 in both eyes, and there are bilateral hypopigmented choroidal lesions and mild vitritis. What blood test is most consistent with the diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
HLA-A29 is associated with birdshot chorioretinopathy in more than 95% of cases, and has a sensitivity of 96% and specificity of 93%. Symptoms include floaters, photopsias, nyctalopia, and decreased contrast sensitivity. The clinical features are characterized by yellow choroidal lesions, vasculitis, and mild vitritis. When the clinical features are suggestive of birdshot, HLA-A29 testing is warranted and, if results are negative, should prompt consideration of another possible etiology or diagnosis. Approximately 7% of the general population will be HLA-A29 positive.
The presence of HLA-B27 is typically evaluated when a patient presents with noninfectious recurrent anterior nongranulomatous uveitis or anterior uveitis that is characterized by hypopyon. The patient will classically be someone with symptoms of a seronegative spondyloarthropathy (ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis, or inflammatory bowel disease).
HLA-DR14 has been associated with some cases of tubulointerstitial nephritis and uveitis (TINU) syndrome.
HLA-B51 is associated with some cases of Behçet disease, especially when there is ocular involvement in Behçet disease.

pool.q: What is the mechanism by which autoimmune regulator (AIRE)-deficient mice, a murine model of uveitis, develop ocular inflammation?

options.a: AIRE-deficient mice do not express cell-type-specific proteins and therefore self-reactive T-cells are not deleted.
options.b: Self-tolerance occurs in the thymus of AIRE-deficient mice.
options.c: AIRE-deficient mice are immunized with interphotoreceptor retinoid binding protein (IRBP).
options.d: AIRE-deficient mice are immunized with retinal S-antigen.

pool.rationale: AIRE-deficient mice lack a transcription factor used by the thymus in the development of T-cell self-tolerance. Consequently, T-cells that may be autoreactive are not deleted and can go on to develop autoimmunity against self antigens, including IRBP, thereby causing posterior uveitis. Thus, self-tolerance does not occur in the thymus of AIRE-deficient mice. Non-AIRE-deficient mice are immunized with retinal S-antigen or IRBP-derived peptides to induce experimental autoimmune uveitis (EAU).

pool.q: For a patient with intermediate uveitis and a recent tick bite, what is the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)–recommended testing protocol for suspected Lyme disease?

options.a: enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for Lyme IgM and IgG antibodies followed by Western immunoblot testing
options.b: polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for Lyme (ie, Borrelia burgdorferi) DNA in aqueous humor
options.c: determinations of Lyme IgM and IgG titers in aqueous humor
options.d: PCR testing for Lyme DNA in vitreous humor

pool.rationale: Lyme disease is diagnosed on the basis of clinical signs, symptoms, and a history of possible exposure. The US CDC currently recommends a 2-step approach to testing for Lyme antibodies: (1) an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (or rarely, an indirect immunofluorescence assay) and (2) an immunoblot (in this case, a Western blot). Both steps can be done using the same blood specimen. If the assay result is negative, no further testing is necessary. Results are considered positive only if both steps test positive. Performing only the Western blot analysis can increase the false-positive rate. Polymerase chain reaction–based assays can be used to amplify Borrelia burgdorferi DNA found in ocular fluids; however, this assay is rarely performed at present.

pool.q: In addition to herpes simplex virus and varicella zoster virus, what member of the herpesvirus family is most likely to cause unilateral anterior uveitis?
pool.rationale:
Viral infections may cause either anterior or posterior uveitis. The most common viruses causing uveitis are cytomegalovirus (CMV), herpes zoster, and herpes simplex. CMV is being increasingly recognized in Asian populations as a cause of a chronic, unilateral anterior uveitis associated with elevated intraocular pressure.
Epstein-Barr virus is the viral agent commonly associated with infectious mononucleosis (IM). A mild, self-limiting follicular conjunctivitis, usually appearing early in the course of the disease, is most common with acquired IM. Less frequently reported anterior ocular manifestations of acquired IM include epithelial or stromal keratitis; episcleritis; and bilateral, granulomatous anterior uveitis.
HHV 6 and 7 do not cause uveitis. They cause a febrile illness in children called roseola that is characterized by high temperatures, followed by a rash that does not desquamate.

pool.q: A 48-year-old woman is referred for glaucoma evaluation. On initial examination, she is found to have intraocular pressure (IOP) of 27 mm Hg OU, corneal pachymetry of 570 OD and 575 OS, and normal results OU from analysis of retinal nerve fiber layer with optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the optic nerve head. What is the best next step in her management, based on findings of the Ocular Hypertension Treatment Study (OHTS)?

options.b: Start ocular hypotensive medical therapy OU.
options.d: Schedule a repeat examination in 1 year.

pool.rationale:
This patient may be a glaucoma suspect based on potential ocular hypertension from her initial IOP readings. Since her OCT appears within normal limits, indicating likely normal anatomic structure of the ONH, it is important to assess her peripheral vision for any early deficits that may be glaucomatous in nature. Visual field testing, or standard automated perimetry (SAP) is used to assess functional changes. In the OHTS, it was found that a higher pattern standard deviation on visual field testing was an important risk factor for development of POAG. Other important risk factors from the OHTS include older age, higher IOP, thinner corneas, and a larger baseline cup-disc ratio.
Until complete testing, including visual field analysis, can be obtained in this patient, starting medical or surgical therapy is not indicated. It is also important to perform all baseline testing before moving to a longer period for follow-up, such as 1 year.

pool.q: A Japanese woman presents with bilateral retinal vasculitis and retinitis. She has a history of painful vaginal ulcerative lesions that have never responded to antiviral therapy. What other feature is needed to classify her as having Behçet disease?

options.a: periventricular white matter lesions on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain
options.c: serologically positive for human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B51
options.d: at least 3 oral aphthous ulcers annually

pool.rationale: The criteria for Behçet disease are entirely clinical. In addition to having at least 3 oral aphthous ulcers each year, a patient must have 2 of the following: ocular inflammation, recurrent genital ulcers, skin lesions (such as erythema nodosum, folliculitis, or acneiform pustules), and a positive cutaneous pathergy test (per the International Study Group for Behçet Disease). While HLA-B51 positivity has been associated with Behçet disease, this test is not part of the diagnostic criteria. Gingival hyperplasia is not associated with Behçet disease, but can be a side effect of cyclosporine. Periventricular white matter lesions on MRI can be seen in multiple sclerosis.
